modules.title: Complexity & arrays
modules.summary: Predict how code scales before you run it, and use two pointers and sliding windows to turn O(n²) array scans into O(n).

lessons.title: Big-O intuition
lessons.objective: By the end you can classify a snippet as O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n) or O(n²) and say what happens to its runtime when n doubles.
concept: Big-O describes how the number of steps an algorithm takes **grows** as the input size `n` grows. It deliberately ignores constant factors and lower-order terms: `3n + 50` and `100n` are both **O(n)**, because for large `n` the shape of the curve matters far more than the constant in front. The practical question Big-O answers is: if I double `n`, what happens to the time? O(1) stays the same, O(log n) adds one step, O(n) doubles, O(n²) quadruples.

You can usually read the class off the shape of the code. A single loop over the input is **O(n)**. Two nested loops that each run over the input are **O(n²)**. A loop that halves the remaining problem each time (like binary search) is **O(log n)**. Doing O(log n) work for each of `n` items, which is what good sorting does, is **O(n log n)**. Indexing a list or looking up a dict key is **O(1)**.

Unless someone says otherwise, "time complexity" means the **worst case**. Use it to predict whether code will finish: CPython does very roughly 10^7 simple operations per second. With `n = 10^5`, an O(n²) algorithm does 10^10 steps, about 15–20 minutes, while O(n log n) is about 1.7 million steps, well under a second. Problem constraints are a hint: `n ≤ 10^5` means the intended solution is O(n log n) or better.

example.explain: `first_item` does one step regardless of size. `contains` may scan the whole list (worst case: target missing), so it is O(n). `has_pair_sum` checks about n²/2 pairs when no pair exists, which is still O(n²) because the 1/2 is a constant. Output: `4 True False`.

lessons.tryit: Time `contains` and `has_pair_sum` with `time.perf_counter()` on lists of size 1,000, 2,000 and 4,000 where the answer is False (the worst case). Write down the ratio between consecutive sizes and check that one roughly doubles and the other roughly quadruples. In one sentence each, explain any ratio that does not match.

questions.prompt: Why is `3n + 50` written as O(n)?
options: Because Big-O keeps only the fastest-growing term and drops constant factors
Because Big-O measures the best case
questions.explain: Big-O describes the growth rate: for large n the `+ 50` becomes irrelevant and the factor 3 does not change the shape of the curve. It is not about the best case (Big-O is usually quoted for the worst case), and comparing to n² does not explain why it is O(n).

questions.prompt: An O(n²) function takes 2 seconds for n = 10,000. Roughly how long for n = 20,000?
questions.explain: Doubling n multiplies n² by 2² = 4, so 2 s × 4 = 8 s. 4 seconds is what an O(n) algorithm would take, and 16 seconds would mean the time grew ×8, which is O(n³) behaviour.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of this function for a list of length n?
questions.explain: The inner loop runs over `nums[:3]`, which has at most 3 elements no matter how large n is, so the body runs at most 3n times: O(n). Nested loops only mean O(n²) when both loops grow with n.

questions.prompt: A problem says `1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5`. Which time complexity should your solution aim for?
questions.explain: At n = 10^5, O(n²) is 10^10 operations, far too slow in Python (minutes). O(n log n) is about 1.7 × 10^6, which runs in well under a second. O(2^n) and O(n³) are even worse than O(n²).

lessons.why: Big-O lets you predict whether code will finish before you run it. It's the first question in every interview and every design review about performance.

terms.d: How the number of steps grows with input size `n`, ignoring constants.
Steps grow by one each time `n` doubles, as in binary search.
Typical of good sorting: a little worse than linear.
The input that makes the algorithm do the most work; the default meaning of 'complexity'.

mistakes.wrong: O(n) code is always faster than O(n²) code.
mistakes.right: For small `n`, constants can win. Big-O describes how runtime grows, not the time for one input.
Constants and lower-order terms are dropped, so it's simply O(n).

takeaways: Read the class from the code's shape: one loop O(n), nested loops O(n²), halving O(log n).
Doubling `n` doubles O(n) work and quadruples O(n²) work.
At about 10^7 simple Python steps per second, you can estimate runtime from n.

lessons.title: Counting operations
lessons.objective: By the end you can derive the Big-O of loops whose bounds depend on each other, loops that halve or double, and code that hides cost inside built-ins.
concept: To find the complexity, count how many times the **innermost line** runs as a function of `n`. For `for i in range(n): for j in range(i):` the inner line runs 0 + 1 + 2 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2 times. That is about n²/2, which is still **O(n²)**: a triangular loop does half the work of a square one, but halving is a constant factor and does not change the class.

When the loop variable multiplies or divides instead of adding, the count is logarithmic. `i = 1; while i < n: i *= 2` runs about log₂ n times, because i reaches n after that many doublings. A loop of `n` iterations that each contain a halving loop is **O(n log n)**. Rules of combination: blocks one after another **add** (O(n) + O(n²) = O(n²), keep the biggest); blocks nested inside each other **multiply**.

Built-ins are not free. `x in some_list` scans the list, `list.pop(0)` and `list.insert(0, x)` shift every element, and slicing `a[i:j]` copies `j − i` elements: all O(n). A loop that calls one of them on every iteration is secretly **O(n²)**. In contrast `x in some_set`, `d[key]` and `list.append` are O(1) on average. When you analyse code, read each line and ask what it costs, not only how many times it runs.

example.explain: Instrumenting a loop with a counter is the fastest way to check your analysis. The triangular loop runs 0+1+…+9 = 45 = 10·9/2 times, and halving 1024 reaches 1 after 10 steps because 2^10 = 1024. Output: `45 10`.

lessons.tryit: Write a function that removes duplicates from a list while keeping order, first using `if x not in result_list`, then using a `seen` set. Add a step counter to the list version, run it on `list(range(n))` for n = 500 and 1,000, and confirm the count roughly quadruples. Then time both versions at n = 20,000.

questions.prompt: Which list operation is O(n) rather than O(1)?
questions.explain: `pop(0)` removes the first element and must shift every remaining element one slot left. `append`, indexing and `len` are O(1) (append is amortized O(1)).

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
steps = 0
i = 1
while i < 100:
    i *= 3
    steps += 1
print(steps)
questions.explain: i goes 1 → 3 → 9 → 27 → 81 → 243. After the fifth multiplication i = 243, the check `243 < 100` fails, so steps = 5. This is log₃(100) rounded up: a multiplying loop is logarithmic.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of this code?
questions.explain: The outer loop runs n times. The inner loop halves j from n down to 0, about log₂ n + 1 iterations. n × log n = O(n log n). It is not O(n²) because the inner loop does not run n times.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of `dedupe`, and what is the fix?
options: O(n²), because `x not in out` scans a list; track seen items in a set to get O(n)
O(n log n), because the list grows gradually
O(1), because each element is touched once
questions.explain: Each `x not in out` scans up to len(out) elements, so with n distinct items the total is 1 + 2 + … + n = O(n²). Keeping a separate `seen` set makes each membership test O(1) on average, giving O(n). The `append` being O(1) is true but irrelevant: the hidden cost is the `in`.

video.title: Time Complexity of Nested Loops (Dependent Loops)

lessons.why: Real code rarely has two neat nested loops. Counting the innermost line, and knowing which built-ins hide loops, catches the O(n²) code that looks O(n).

terms.d: The statement that runs most often; count its executions as a function of n.
`for j in range(i)` inside `for i in range(n)`: about n²/2 runs, still O(n²).
A loop variable that doubles or halves: about log₂ n iterations.
Built-ins like `x in list`, `pop(0)` and slicing that are O(n) each call.

mistakes.wrong: A loop that calls `list.pop(0)` once per iteration is O(n).
mistakes.right: Each `pop(0)` shifts every element, so the loop is O(n²). Use `collections.deque`.

mistakes.wrong: Sequential loops multiply: two loops over n are O(n²).
mistakes.right: Loops one after another add (O(n) + O(n) = O(n)); only nested loops multiply.

takeaways: Count how many times the innermost line runs.
Nested loops multiply, sequential loops add.
`in` on a list, `pop(0)`, `insert(0, x)` and slices are O(n) each.

lessons.title: Space complexity
lessons.objective: By the end you can state the extra space a function uses, including recursion stack depth, and choose deliberately between saving time and saving memory.
concept: Space complexity counts the **extra memory** an algorithm allocates as `n` grows, usually excluding the input itself ("auxiliary space"). A few integer variables are **O(1)**, however large the numbers. Building a new list of size n, a set of seen values, or a dict of counts is **O(n)**. An n × n table of results is **O(n²)**: at n = 10^4 that is 10^8 cells, which will not fit comfortably in memory even before you think about time.

Recursion uses space even when you allocate nothing: every call that has not returned yet keeps a **stack frame**. A recursive sum that recurses once per element has n frames alive at its deepest point, so it is O(n) space. Python's default recursion limit is 1000 (`sys.getrecursionlimit()`), so depth-n recursion on 10^5 items raises `RecursionError`. Slicing in recursion, as in `f(nums[1:])`, also copies the list every call: O(n²) total copying.

Time and space trade against each other. A `seen` set costs O(n) memory but turns an O(n²) duplicate check into O(n). Sorting first and comparing neighbours uses O(n log n) time with little extra memory, but mutates the input if you use `list.sort()`. When an interviewer asks "can you do it in O(1) extra space?", they usually want two pointers or reusing the input array as storage.

left.title: Set of seen values
points: O(n) extra space for the set

right.title: Sort, then compare neighbours
points: No extra structure beyond the sort's own buffer

example.explain: Both functions are O(n) time, but `sum_rec` is O(n) space because each element adds a stack frame, while `sum_iter` is O(1) space: one accumulator. Output: `10 12497500`.

lessons.tryit: Write `has_duplicate_set(a)` and `has_duplicate_sorted(a)` (sort a copy, then compare neighbours). For each, write its time and extra-space complexity in a comment. Then call `sum_rec` on lists of growing length until it raises `RecursionError`, and note the length where it fails.

questions.prompt: What does "auxiliary space" leave out of the count?
questions.explain: Auxiliary space is the extra memory beyond the input. Stack frames and local variables are part of it. Output is often counted too, though some authors exclude it; the input is the thing that is consistently excluded.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
c = a[:]
a.append(4)
print(len(b), len(c))
questions.explain: `b = a` copies no data, it is a second name for the same list, so it sees the append. `a[:]` allocates a new list (O(n) space and time), which keeps its 3 items. Knowing which operations allocate is the core of space analysis.

questions.prompt: What is the extra space used by this recursive binary search on a list of length n?
questions.explain: Each call halves the range, so at most about log₂ n calls are on the stack at once: O(log n) space. An iterative version with a `while` loop would be O(1). It is not O(n) because no slices are copied; only indices are passed.

questions.prompt: You must decide whether any two numbers in a list of 10^6 integers sum to a target. Memory is too tight for a hash set of all the values, and O(n²) is too slow. Which approach fits?
options: Sort the list in place, then walk two pointers inward from both ends
Insert every value into a dict and look up `target - x`
Recursively split the list in half and check each half
questions.explain: Sorting in place costs O(n log n) time and no new structure, and the two-pointer walk is O(n) time and O(1) space. The dict approach is O(n) time but needs O(n) memory, which the constraint rules out. Nested loops are 5 × 10^11 pair checks. Splitting into halves misses pairs that straddle the split.

lessons.why: Memory is a budget too. Knowing the extra space your code uses, including the recursion stack, prevents crashes and lets you trade memory for speed on purpose.

terms.d: Extra memory allocated as n grows, not counting the input.
Memory held by each call that hasn't returned yet.
How many frames are alive at once; Python's default limit is about 1,000.
Spending memory (like a `seen` set) to save time, or the reverse.

mistakes.wrong: A recursive function that allocates nothing uses O(1) space.
mistakes.right: Each pending call keeps a frame, so recursing n deep is O(n) space.

mistakes.wrong: Big integers make a few variables use O(n) space.
mistakes.right: We count variables that grow with n. A fixed number of integer variables is O(1).

takeaways: Count new lists, sets, dicts and recursion depth as n grows.
Deep recursion costs memory and can hit the recursion limit.
Choose the trade-off deliberately: a `seen` set turns O(n²) into O(n) for O(n) memory.

lessons.title: Two pointers
lessons.objective: By the end you can solve sorted pair-sum, palindrome and in-place compaction problems in O(n) time and O(1) extra space with two pointers.
concept: Two pointers means keeping two indices that move through the array according to a rule, so each element is visited a constant number of times: **O(n)** instead of checking all O(n²) pairs. In the **opposite-ends** pattern, `l` starts at 0 and `r` at `len(a) - 1`, and they move toward each other. It works when one comparison tells you which pointer to move, which is true for sorted arrays and for symmetric checks like palindromes.

Pair sum in a sorted array: if `a[l] + a[r]` is too small, the only way to grow the sum is to move `l` right; if too big, move `r` left. The correctness argument: when the sum is too small, `a[l]` paired with anything at or left of `r` is also too small, so `a[l]` can be discarded forever. Every step discards one element, so there are at most n − 1 steps.

In the **same-direction** (slow/fast) pattern, `fast` scans every element while `slow` marks where the next kept element should be written. Removing duplicates from a sorted array, moving zeros to the end, and partitioning all work this way in O(n) time and O(1) space. Both patterns replace a nested loop with a single pass. Cue words that suggest two pointers: **sorted**, **in place**, **pair** or **triplet**, **palindrome**, "O(1) extra space".

visual.title: Pair summing to 8 in a sorted list

example.explain: `slow` always points at the last unique value written. When `fast` finds a new value, `slow` advances and the value is copied there. The first k slots end up holding the unique values; the rest of the list is leftover. Output: `4 [1, 2, 3, 4]`.

lessons.tryit: Write `is_palindrome(s)` that ignores case and non-alphanumeric characters using two pointers and no new string (use `str.isalnum()` and `str.lower()`). Test it on "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" and "race a car". Then solve LeetCode 167 (Two Sum II) and write the one-sentence correctness argument as a comment.

questions.prompt: What property of the input makes the opposite-ends pair-sum technique correct?
questions.explain: Sorted order is what guarantees that moving `l` right can only increase the sum and moving `r` left can only decrease it. Duplicates, length parity and sign do not matter.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
a = [0, 1, 0, 3, 12]
slow = 0
for fast in range(len(a)):
    if a[fast] != 0:
        a[slow], a[fast] = a[fast], a[slow]
        slow += 1
print(a)
questions.explain: Each non-zero value is swapped down to position `slow`, which then advances. The non-zero values keep their relative order (1, 3, 12) and the zeros drift to the end. One pass, O(1) extra space.

questions.prompt: Arrange the lines to return True if `s` reads the same forwards and backwards, using two pointers.
questions.explain: Initialise both ends, compare before moving, then step both pointers inward. Moving the pointers before the comparison would skip the outermost pair, so a string like "xaa" would wrongly pass.

questions.prompt: A teammate runs the opposite-ends pair-sum loop on the unsorted list `[4, 1, 5, 2]` with target 3, and it reports that no pair exists, even though 1 + 2 = 3. What went wrong?
options: The loop condition should be `l <= r`
Without sorted order, moving a pointer does not reliably raise or lower the sum, so the pair can be skipped
Two pointers cannot handle a target smaller than the first element
The list needs an even number of elements
questions.explain: Trace it: 4+2=6 is too big, so r moves left; 4+5=9, r moves; 4+1=5, r moves and meets l. The discard argument assumed sorted order. Changing the condition to `l <= r` would just pair an element with itself. Sort first (or use a hash map) to fix it.

lessons.why: Two pointers turns many 'check every pair' problems from O(n²) into one O(n) pass with no extra memory. It's one of the most common interview patterns.

terms.d: `l` from the start and `r` from the end, moving inward.
`fast` scans everything while `slow` marks where to write the next kept item.
Changing the array itself instead of building a new one: O(1) extra space.
A statement that stays true every step, such as 'no answer lies outside l..r'.

mistakes.wrong: Two pointers works for pair sums on any array.
mistakes.right: The opposite-ends version relies on sorted order to know which pointer to move.

mistakes.wrong: Moving either pointer is fine when the sum is wrong.
mistakes.right: If the sum is too small, only moving `l` right can increase it; moving `r` would skip valid pairs.

takeaways: Each pointer only moves forward, so every element is visited a constant number of times.
Opposite ends for sorted pair problems and palindromes; same direction for compaction.
Be able to say why moving a pointer can't skip the answer.

lessons.title: Sliding window
lessons.objective: By the end you can recognise contiguous-subarray problems and solve both fixed-size and variable-size window problems in O(n).
concept: A window is a contiguous range `a[l..r]`. For "maximum sum of any k consecutive elements", recomputing each window from scratch costs O(n·k). Sliding is cheaper: when the window moves one step right, **add the element that enters and subtract the one that leaves**. Each step is O(1), so the whole scan is O(n). This is the fixed-size window, and the same idea works for averages, counts of a character, or any state you can update incrementally.

In a **variable-size window**, `r` advances on every iteration to expand the window. Whenever the window breaks the rule (a repeated character, a sum that is too large), shrink it from the left with `l += 1` until the rule holds again, then record the answer. There is a `while` inside the `for`, but it is still **O(n)**: each index enters the window once and leaves at most once, so the total number of moves of `l` and `r` together is at most 2n.

When does it apply? The answer must be **contiguous**, and validity must be monotonic: if a window is invalid, any bigger window containing it is also invalid. Smallest subarray with sum ≥ target works when all numbers are positive. With negative numbers adding an element can shrink the sum, monotonicity breaks, and you need prefix sums with a hash map (next module) instead. Keep the window's state in a set, a counter dict or a running sum.

steps.label: Expand
steps.detail: Move r one step right and add a[r] to the window state

steps.label: Check
steps.detail: Does the window now break the rule?

steps.label: Shrink
steps.detail: While it does, remove a[l] from the state and do l += 1

steps.label: Record
steps.detail: Update the best answer using the window length r − l + 1

steps.label: Repeat
steps.detail: Each index is added once and removed once: O(n) total

example.code:
def longest_unique(s):
    seen = set()
    l = best = 0
    for r, ch in enumerate(s):
        while ch in seen:
            seen.remove(s[l])
            l += 1
        seen.add(ch)
        best = max(best, r - l + 1)
    return best

print(longest_unique("abcabcbb"), longest_unique("pwwkew"))
example.explain: The set holds exactly the characters in the window. When `ch` is already inside, characters are dropped from the left until the old copy of `ch` is gone. For "abcabcbb" the best window is "abc"; for "pwwkew" it is "wke". Output: `3 3`.

lessons.tryit: Write `max_sum_k(nums, k)` with a fixed window, and `min_len_at_least(target, nums)` (LeetCode 209) with a variable window. Write brute-force versions of both, then compare them on 1,000 random lists of positive integers with `assert`. Finally, try `min_len_at_least` on a list containing negative numbers and find an input where it gives the wrong answer.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a sliding-window problem?
options: Longest contiguous substring with at most 2 distinct characters
Do any two numbers anywhere in the list sum to 10?
Count all subsets that sum to 10
questions.explain: Only the first asks about a contiguous range whose validity is monotonic (adding characters can only add distinct ones). Pairs anywhere in the list call for a hash map or two pointers on sorted data; k-th largest calls for a heap or quickselect; subsets are not contiguous at all.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
nums = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]
k = 3
window = sum(nums[:k])
best = window
for i in range(k, len(nums)):
    window += nums[i] - nums[i - k]
    best = max(best, window)
print(best)
questions.explain: The window sums are 2+1+5=8, 1+5+1=7, 5+1+3=9 and 1+3+2=6. Each step adds `nums[i]` and drops `nums[i - k]`, so the maximum, 9, is found in O(n).

questions.prompt: `longest_unique` has a `while` loop nested inside a `for` loop. What is its time complexity for a string of length n?
options: O(n·k) where k is the window size
questions.explain: `l` only ever moves right and never past `r`, so across the whole run the inner loop executes at most n times in total. Together with the n iterations of the outer loop that is O(n). Nested loops are not automatically O(n²); count the total work.

questions.prompt: Why does the shrink-while-the-sum-is-too-big window give wrong answers when the array contains negative numbers?
options: Negative numbers cannot be stored in the running sum
Adding an element can lower the sum, so a window that is too small to be valid might become valid by growing, and shrinking can make it worse; validity is no longer monotonic
The window would need to move right to left
Python's `max` does not handle negative numbers
questions.explain: The technique assumes that growing the window only moves the sum one way. With negatives that assumption fails, so discarding the left element can throw away part of the best answer. Use prefix sums plus a hash map for subarray-sum problems with negatives.

lessons.why: Contiguous-range questions (best streak, longest substring, smallest subarray) come up constantly in data processing and interviews. Sliding a window makes them O(n).

terms.d: A contiguous range `a[l..r]`.
Slide by adding the entering element and subtracting the leaving one.
Grow with `r`, shrink from the left while the rule is broken.
If a window is invalid, every larger window containing it is too.

mistakes.wrong: Sliding window works for any subarray-sum problem.
mistakes.right: With negative numbers, shrinking can increase the sum, so validity isn't monotonic. Use prefix sums instead.

mistakes.wrong: A variable window with an inner `while` loop is O(n²).
mistakes.right: `l` only moves forward, at most n times in total, so the whole thing is O(n).

takeaways: Only contiguous answers fit a window.
Update the window in O(1) per step instead of recomputing it.
Check monotonic validity before choosing this pattern.

project.title: Complexity benchmark harness
project.brief: Build a script that times functions over growing input sizes and prints each size, the time and the ratio to the previous size. Seeing an O(n) column double while an O(n²) column quadruples turns Big-O from notation into something you can measure.
milestones: Write `bench(fn, make_input, sizes)` that runs each size 5 times with `time.perf_counter()` and keeps the minimum time.
Implement `has_duplicate_quadratic` (nested loops) and `has_duplicate_set`; assert they agree on 200 random lists before timing anything.
Time both on sizes 1,000, 2,000, 4,000, 8,000 using lists with no duplicates (the worst case) and print a table with the doubling ratio; confirm ≈2 versus ≈4.
Add a sliding-window `max_sum_k` and its O(n·k) brute force with k = n // 10, and explain in a comment why the brute force's ratio is about 4.
Estimate the exponent as log₂(t₂ / t₁) for each pair of rows and print the guessed class (O(n), O(n log n), O(n²)).
project.stretch: Plot the results with matplotlib on log–log axes and fit a line to each series; the slope is the exponent.

exam.prompt: What is the time complexity of this function?
exam.explain: `a.sort()` is O(n log n) and the scan is O(n). Sequential blocks add, and n log n dominates n. The loop alone would be O(n), but you must count the cost of the built-in too.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: For i = 0, 1, 2, 3 the inner loop runs 4, 3, 2, 1 times: 10 = 4·5/2. A triangular loop like this is O(n²) in general.

exam.prompt: Given a sorted list that may contain negatives, such as `[-4, -1, 0, 3, 10]`, return the squares in sorted order. Which approach gives O(n)?
options: Two pointers at both ends: the larger absolute value produces the next-largest square, filling the result from the back
Binary search for zero, then sort each half
exam.explain: The largest square is always at one of the two ends, so comparing `abs(a[l])` and `abs(a[r])` picks the next-largest square in O(1): O(n) total. Squaring and sorting works but is O(n log n). A window of size 2 does not order anything.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.code:
nums = [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3]
l = total = 0
best = len(nums) + 1
for r in range(len(nums)):
    total += nums[r]
    while total >= 7:
        best = min(best, r - l + 1)
        total -= nums[l]
        l += 1
print(best)
exam.explain: This is the smallest window with sum ≥ 7. The windows that reach 7 are [2,3,1,2], [3,1,2,4] → shrinks to [1,2,4], then [2,4,3] → shrinks to [4,3]. The shortest is [4, 3], length 2.

exam.prompt: Both `a` and `b` have length n. What is the complexity of this line, and how do you make it O(n)?
exam.code: only_in_a = [x for x in a if x not in b]
options: O(n²), because `x not in b` scans the list b for every x; build `bs = set(b)` first and test `x not in bs`
O(n log n), because comprehensions sort internally
O(1), because comprehensions run in C
exam.explain: The comprehension runs n times and each `in` on a list is O(n): O(n²) total. Converting `b` to a set once is O(n), and each membership test becomes O(1) on average, for O(n) overall. Comprehensions are faster than hand loops by a constant factor, not by a complexity class.

exam.prompt: A problem's constraints say `n ≤ 20`. What does that suggest about the intended solution?
options: An exponential solution such as O(2^n) or O(n·2^n) is acceptable
exam.explain: 2^20 is about 10^6, which runs quickly, so tiny limits usually signal that trying every subset (backtracking or bitmasks) is intended. Large limits like 10^5 are the ones that demand O(n log n) or better.

exam.prompt: For Two Sum on an unsorted list, where you must return the original indices, why is a hash map usually preferred over sort + two pointers?
options: Two pointers do not work on integers
The hash map is O(n), while sorting costs O(n log n) and scrambles the original indices unless you also store them
The hash map uses less memory
Sorting is not allowed on lists
exam.explain: The dict of value → index finds the complement in one O(n) pass. Sort + two pointers is O(n log n) and needs extra bookkeeping to recover indices, though it does use less memory, which is why the hash map is not chosen for memory reasons.

modules.title: Hashing & linear structures
modules.summary: Know how hash maps, sets, stacks, queues and linked lists work inside, and pick the one that makes a problem O(n).

lessons.title: Hash maps: how they work
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain how a hash map finds a key in O(1) on average, what collisions and resizing are, and why its worst case is O(n).
concept: A hash map stores key → value pairs in an array of **buckets**. To find a key, it computes `hash(key)`, an integer derived from the key, and takes `hash(key) % capacity` to pick a bucket. Then it only has to compare against the few entries in that one bucket. If the entries are spread evenly so each bucket holds about one item, lookup, insert and delete cost **O(1) on average**, however many keys the map holds.

A **collision** happens when two different keys land in the same bucket. With **separate chaining**, each bucket is a small list of (key, value) pairs that you scan. With **open addressing**, used by CPython's `dict`, a colliding key probes other slots in the array until it finds a free one. Either way, if every key landed in the same bucket, each lookup would scan all n entries: the **worst case is O(n)**, which is why a good hash function matters.

The **load factor** is items ÷ buckets. When it passes a threshold (0.75 in Java's HashMap, about 2/3 in CPython's dict), the map allocates a larger array and re-inserts every entry. That one insert costs O(n), but it happens rarely enough that inserts are **amortized O(1)**. Keys must be **hashable**, which for built-ins means immutable: a list key raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`, because mutating it would change its hash and strand it in the wrong bucket. Use a tuple instead.

visual.title: A chained map with 4 buckets (keys are ints, so hash(k) == k)

items.label: Bucket 1
items.detail: (1, 'a') → (5, 'e') → (9, 'i'): three keys collide, so get(9) scans a chain of 3

items.label: Load factor
items.detail: 5 items ÷ 4 buckets = 1.25, above a 0.75 threshold, so a real map would already have doubled to 8 buckets and re-inserted everything

example.explain: In CPython, a small int hashes to itself, so 1, 5 and 9 all give `% 4 == 1` and chain in bucket 1. `get` hashes the key, jumps to one bucket and compares keys only there. Output: `[(1, 1), (5, 25), (9, 81)] 81`.

lessons.tryit: Extend `ChainedMap` with a `size` counter and a `_resize` method that doubles the bucket count when `size / len(buckets) > 0.75`, re-inserting every pair. Insert `range(20)` and print the bucket lengths after each resize. Then write a class whose `__hash__` returns 0 and count how many key comparisons `get` makes with 1,000 such keys.

questions.prompt: In a hash map, what is a collision?
options: Two different keys map to the same bucket
The same key is inserted twice
The map runs out of memory
questions.explain: A collision is two distinct keys landing in the same bucket. Inserting the same key twice is just an update; collisions are normal and handled by chaining or probing.

questions.prompt: In CPython, a small int hashes to itself. What does this print?
questions.code: print(hash(7) % 4, hash(11) % 4)
questions.explain: hash(7) is 7 and hash(11) is 11; both leave remainder 3 when divided by 4, so in a 4-bucket map these keys collide in bucket 3.

questions.prompt: What happens when this line runs?
options: It creates a dict with one entry
The list is converted to a tuple automatically
questions.explain: Lists are mutable, so they are not hashable and cannot be dict keys or set members. Python never converts them silently; use the tuple `(1, 2)` as the key instead.

questions.prompt: A class defines `__hash__` to always return 42. You put 10,000 instances in a dict. What happens to lookup time, and why?
options: Still O(1): dicts always hash in constant time
It degrades to O(n): every key lands in the same place, so a lookup must compare against many keys
It raises an error because hashes must be unique
It becomes O(log n) because dicts switch to a tree
questions.explain: Equal hashes are legal (only equal objects must have equal hashes), so nothing errors. But all keys collide, and finding one key means comparing it against the colliding entries: O(n) per lookup. CPython does not switch to a tree; Java's HashMap does that for long chains, which gives O(log n) there.

lessons.why: Dicts and sets are the most-used data structures in Python. Knowing how hashing works explains why they're fast, when they're not, and why keys must be immutable.

terms.d: Turns a key into an integer; `hash(key) % capacity` picks a bucket.
Two keys landing in the same bucket.
Items ÷ buckets; past a threshold the table resizes.
Occasional expensive resizes averaged over many cheap inserts.

mistakes.wrong: Hash map lookups are always O(1).
mistakes.right: They're O(1) on average. If many keys collide, a lookup degrades toward O(n).

mistakes.wrong: I can use a list as a dict key if I don't change it.
mistakes.right: Lists aren't hashable at all. Use a tuple for compound keys.

takeaways: Hashing picks a bucket, so a lookup compares against only a few entries.
Resizing keeps the load factor low, making inserts amortized O(1).
Keys must be hashable: immutable values like strings, numbers and tuples.

lessons.title: Sets & frequency counting
lessons.objective: By the end you can use sets, counting dicts and the complement trick to replace nested loops with a single O(n) pass.
concept: A **set** is a hash map with keys and no values: `add`, `remove` and `x in s` are O(1) on average. Reach for one whenever the question is "have I seen this before?": deduplicating, detecting a repeat, checking membership against a large collection. Set algebra comes free: `a & b` (in both), `a | b` (in either), `a - b` (in a but not b). Building a set from a list is O(n), so it pays off as soon as you would otherwise scan the list repeatedly.

**Frequency counting** maps each item to how many times it appears. By hand: `counts[x] = counts.get(x, 0) + 1`. Or use `collections.Counter(iterable)`, which also offers `most_common(k)` and comparison with `==`. Two strings are anagrams exactly when their counters are equal, which is O(n) instead of the O(n log n) of sorting both strings. Grouping is counting's cousin: `groups.setdefault(key, []).append(item)` builds lists of items that share a key.

The **complement trick**: scanning once, ask whether the partner you need has already appeared. Two Sum keeps a dict `value → index` and checks `target - x in seen` before inserting x: one pass, O(n). The same idea with **prefix sums** counts subarrays summing to k even with negative numbers: keep counts of every prefix sum seen; at prefix p, add `counts[p - k]` to the answer. That handles exactly the negative-number case that breaks a sliding window.

visual.title: Two Sum with a dict, target 9

example.explain: Counters compare equal when every character has the same count. For grouping, every anagram sorts to the same key ("aet" for eat, tea and ate), and `setdefault` creates the list the first time a key appears. Output: `True [['eat', 'tea', 'ate'], ['tan', 'nat'], ['bat']]`.

lessons.tryit: Solve LeetCode 560 (Subarray Sum Equals K) with prefix sums and a Counter, starting from `counts = {0: 1}`. Before coding, work through `nums = [1, -1, 1, 1]`, k = 2 by hand, writing the prefix sums and the counts dict after each step. Then explain in two sentences why a sliding window cannot solve this input.

questions.prompt: What is the average time complexity of `x in s` when `s` is a set of n items?
questions.explain: Membership hashes x and checks one bucket: O(1) on average. O(n) is the cost of `x in some_list`, and also the theoretical worst case for a set if every item collided.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
from collections import Counter
print(Counter("banana").most_common(1))
questions.explain: "banana" has a×3, n×2, b×1. `most_common(1)` returns a list holding the single (item, count) pair with the highest count.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: `a - b` keeps what is in a but not in b, and `a & b` keeps what is in both. `sorted` turns each set into an ordered list, because a set's own print order is not something to rely on.

questions.prompt: Count the contiguous subarrays of `[3, -2, 4, -1, 2]` (values may be negative) whose sum equals 5. Which approach is correct and O(n)?
options: A sliding window that shrinks whenever the sum exceeds 5
Prefix sums with a hash map counting how often each prefix sum has occurred
Sort the list and use two pointers
A set of all values, checking `5 - x`
questions.explain: Subarray sum = prefix[j] − prefix[i], so at each prefix p you need how many earlier prefixes equal p − 5: a counting dict answers that in O(1). The window fails because negatives break monotonicity. Sorting destroys contiguity, and the set checks pairs of values, not subarrays.

lessons.why: 'Have I seen this?' and 'how many of each?' replace whole nested loops. These two habits alone fix a large share of slow beginner code.

terms.d: A hash map of keys only, with O(1) average `add` and `in`.
Mapping each item to how often it appears, by hand or with `Counter`.
Before adding x, check whether `target - x` has already been seen.
Running total; counting prefix sums finds subarrays with a given sum.

mistakes.wrong: Two Sum needs a nested loop over all pairs.
mistakes.right: One pass with a dict of seen values checks each complement in O(1), so it's O(n).

mistakes.wrong: For Two Sum I can add all numbers to the dict first, then look for complements.
mistakes.right: Then `x` can match itself. Check for the complement before inserting `x`.

takeaways: Use a set for membership and duplicates.
`Counter` compares multisets, which makes anagram checks one line.
The complement trick turns pair searches into one pass.

lessons.title: Stacks & the monotonic stack
lessons.objective: By the end you can use a stack for nesting problems and a monotonic stack to find the next greater or smaller element for every position in O(n).
concept: A **stack** is last-in, first-out. A Python list is a perfect stack: `append` pushes, `pop()` pops and `stack[-1]` peeks, all O(1). Stacks fit anything with **nesting** or **undo**: matching brackets, evaluating expressions, a browser's back button, and simulating recursion (the call stack is a stack). For brackets, push every opener; on a closer, the top of the stack must be the matching opener, and at the end the stack must be empty.

A **monotonic stack** keeps its contents in sorted order (always decreasing, or always increasing). When a new element would break that order, pop until it does not. Every element you pop has just met its **next greater element**: the new one. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the whole pass is **O(n)**, replacing the O(n²) approach of scanning to the right from every position.

Store **indices** on the stack rather than values, so you can compute distances ("how many days until a warmer temperature?") and still look the value up with `nums[i]`. A stack kept decreasing finds the next greater element; kept increasing it finds the next smaller. Cue words: "next greater", "next smaller", "days until", "stock span", "largest rectangle in a histogram". Indices still on the stack at the end have no answer, so initialise results to a default such as −1 or 0.

visual.title: Next greater element of [2, 1, 3] with a decreasing stack of indices

steps.label: i = 0, value 2
steps.detail: Stack empty, push 0 → stack [0]

steps.label: i = 1, value 1
steps.detail: 1 is not greater than nums[0] = 2, push 1 → stack [0, 1]

steps.label: i = 2, value 3
steps.detail: 3 > nums[1]: pop 1, res[1] = 3. 3 > nums[0]: pop 0, res[0] = 3. Push 2 → stack [2]

steps.label: End
steps.detail: Index 2 is left on the stack, so it has no greater element: res = [3, 3, -1]

example.explain: Openers are pushed. A closer must match the most recent unmatched opener, which is the top of the stack. "([)]" fails because `)` arrives when `[` is on top, and "((" fails because openers remain at the end. Output: `True False False`.

lessons.tryit: Solve LeetCode 739 (Daily Temperatures) with a monotonic stack of indices, then write a brute-force version with nested loops and compare both on 500 random lists. Finally, adapt your code to compute the **previous smaller** element for each index and test it on `[4, 5, 2, 10, 8]` (expected `[-1, 4, -1, 2, 2]`).

questions.prompt: Which pair of Python list operations gives a stack with O(1) push and pop?
questions.explain: Pushing and popping at the end of a list is O(1). Any operation at index 0 shifts every element, which is O(n). `append` with `pop(0)` would also be a queue, not a stack.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
temps = [30, 40, 35, 50]
ans = [0] * len(temps)
stack = []
for i, t in enumerate(temps):
    while stack and temps[stack[-1]] < t:
        j = stack.pop()
        ans[j] = i - j
    stack.append(i)
print(ans)
questions.explain: Day 0 (30) is beaten by day 1: wait 1. Day 1 (40) stays on the stack through day 2 (35) and is beaten by day 3 (50): wait 2. Day 2 is beaten by day 3: wait 1. Day 3 never sees a warmer day, so it keeps the default 0.

questions.prompt: Arrange the lines to return, for each element, the next element to its right that is greater (or -1).
questions.explain: The while loop pops every index whose value is smaller than x, since x is their next greater element, and only then is i pushed. Pushing i before the while loop would make the stack's top always be i itself, so nothing would ever be popped.

questions.prompt: A monotonic-stack solution has a `while` loop inside a `for` loop over n elements. What is its time complexity?
options: O(n²), because the loops are nested
O(n), because each index is pushed once and popped at most once
O(n log n), because the stack stays sorted
questions.explain: Count total work instead of multiplying loop bounds: there are n pushes, and there can be at most n pops in total across all iterations of the while loop. That is O(n). The stack is sorted, but no sorting work is done to keep it that way.

lessons.why: Stacks handle anything nested, from brackets to undo history. The monotonic stack answers 'next greater element' questions in one pass that would otherwise be O(n²).

terms.d: Last in, first out. A Python list with `append` and `pop()`.
Structures where the most recent opening is closed first, like brackets.
A stack kept sorted; popping reveals each element's next greater or smaller value.
Storing positions so you can compute distances and still read values.

mistakes.wrong: Popping in a loop inside a loop makes the monotonic stack O(n²).
mistakes.right: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total is O(n).

mistakes.wrong: Storing values on the stack is enough.
mistakes.right: You often need distances or positions, so store indices and look values up.

takeaways: Reach for a stack when the most recent item matters most.
Decreasing stack finds next greater; increasing finds next smaller.
Push and pop each element once: O(n).

lessons.title: Queues & deque
lessons.objective: By the end you can choose between list and deque, use deque as a queue or bounded buffer, and solve sliding-window maximum with a monotonic deque.
concept: A **queue** is first-in, first-out. Using a list with `pop(0)` works but costs O(n) per dequeue, because every remaining element shifts left; draining a queue of n items that way is O(n²). `collections.deque` supports `append`, `appendleft`, `pop` and `popleft` in **O(1)** at both ends. The trade-off: indexing into the middle of a deque, such as `dq[len(dq) // 2]`, is O(n), so it is not a drop-in replacement when you need random access.

Queues model "handle things in arrival order": breadth-first search (module 5), task schedulers, rate limiters, buffering a stream. `deque(maxlen=k)` is a **bounded buffer**: once it holds k items, appending on one end silently drops an item from the other end. That is exactly "keep the last k log lines" or "moving average of the last k readings", with no manual trimming code.

A **monotonic deque** solves sliding-window maximum in O(n). Keep indices whose values are decreasing from front to back. For each new index: pop from the back while the back's value is ≤ the new value (they can never be the maximum again), append the new index, and pop from the front if it has slid out of the window. The front is always the current window's maximum. The brute force recomputes `max` of every window: O(n·k).

example.explain: Smaller values behind a new larger value are popped because they can never be a window maximum again. The front index leaves when it falls out of the window `[i - k + 1, i]`. Each index enters and leaves the deque once: O(n). Output: `[3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]`.

lessons.tryit: Time draining a queue of 100,000 items with `list.pop(0)` versus `deque.popleft()` and record both times. Then write a `MovingAverage(k)` class with `deque(maxlen=k)` and a running sum, so each `next(value)` call is O(1); subtract the value that is about to be evicted before you append.

questions.prompt: Why prefer `deque.popleft()` over `list.pop(0)` for a queue?
options: `popleft` is O(1); `pop(0)` is O(n) because the list shifts every element
Lists cannot hold more than 1,000 items
questions.explain: Both remove the first element, so the result is the same; the difference is cost. A deque has no need to shift elements, so removing from the left is O(1).

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
from collections import deque
q = deque([1, 2, 3], maxlen=3)
q.append(4)
q.appendleft(0)
print(list(q))
questions.explain: The deque is full, so `append(4)` drops from the left: [2, 3, 4]. `appendleft(0)` on a full deque drops from the right: [0, 2, 3]. A bounded deque always evicts from the end opposite to the one you add to.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of draining a list of n items with this loop?
questions.explain: Each `pop(0)` shifts the remaining items: (n−1) + (n−2) + … + 0 shifts, which is O(n²). With `deque.popleft()` the same loop is O(n).

questions.prompt: A browser needs Back and Forward buttons. Visiting a new page clears the Forward history. Which structure fits best?
options: Two stacks: one for back history, one for forward
A min-heap ordered by visit time
questions.explain: Back returns the most recently visited page, which is last-in, first-out: push the current page onto the forward stack and pop from the back stack. Visiting a new page clears the forward stack. A queue would return the oldest page, and a set has no order at all.

lessons.why: Processing things in arrival order is everywhere: BFS, job queues, rate limiters. Using the right structure keeps a queue O(1) per operation instead of O(n).

terms.d: First in, first out.
Double-ended queue with O(1) append and pop at both ends.
`deque(maxlen=k)`: keeps the last k items, dropping the oldest.
Keeps indices in decreasing value order to track a sliding-window maximum.

mistakes.wrong: A list with `pop(0)` is a fine queue.
mistakes.right: Each `pop(0)` is O(n), so draining n items is O(n²). Use `deque.popleft()`.

mistakes.wrong: Sliding-window maximum needs re-scanning each window.
mistakes.right: A monotonic deque gives each window's maximum in amortized O(1).

takeaways: Use `collections.deque` for queues.
`maxlen` gives you a ring buffer for free.
Drop items from the back that can never be the maximum again.

lessons.title: Linked lists
lessons.objective: By the end you can reverse a linked list, find its middle, and detect a cycle, managing next-pointers without losing nodes.
concept: A **singly linked list** is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a `next` reference to the following node; the list itself is just a reference to the head. Inserting or deleting right after a node you already hold is **O(1)**: re-point one or two references. Reaching index k is **O(k)**, because you must walk from the head. That is the opposite trade-off from arrays, which index in O(1) but shift O(n) elements to insert at the front.

Nearly every linked-list bug is losing the rest of the list. Before overwriting `curr.next`, save it: reversal keeps `prev` and `curr`, stores `nxt = curr.next`, sets `curr.next = prev`, then advances both. A **dummy head** node, a placeholder before the real head, removes special cases when the head itself may change, as in merging two lists or deleting the first node. You return `dummy.next` at the end.

**Fast and slow pointers**: slow moves one node per step and fast moves two. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle. If the list has a cycle, fast eventually laps slow and they meet (Floyd's algorithm): cycle detection in O(n) time and **O(1) space**, compared with O(n) for a set of visited nodes. Production Python rarely needs hand-written linked lists, but interviews use them to test careful reference handling.

steps.label: Start
steps.detail: prev = None, curr = node 1

steps.label: Save, then flip
steps.detail: nxt = curr.next; curr.next = prev

steps.label: Advance
steps.detail: prev = curr; curr = nxt

steps.label: Repeat
steps.detail: Loop until curr is None: 1 → None, then 2 → 1, then 3 → 2

steps.label: Done
steps.detail: prev is the new head: 3 → 2 → 1

example.explain: Each iteration flips one arrow and then steps forward using the saved `nxt`. When `curr` falls off the end, `prev` is the old tail, now the head. O(n) time, O(1) extra space. Output: `[3, 2, 1]`.

lessons.tryit: Implement `merge_two(a, b)` that merges two sorted linked lists using a dummy head, and `has_cycle(head)` with fast and slow pointers. Draw the pointers on paper for one iteration of each before coding. Test `has_cycle` by linking the tail of a 5-node list back to node 2.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of reading the k-th element of a singly linked list?
questions.explain: You must follow k `next` references from the head, since nodes are not stored contiguously. O(1) indexing is what arrays offer.

questions.prompt: Arrange the lines to reverse a singly linked list in place and return the new head.
questions.explain: Save `curr.next` first, then flip the arrow, then advance. Flipping before saving loses the rest of the list, and advancing before flipping never changes any arrow.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: Prepending 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 builds 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5. Fast visits 1, 3, 5 while slow visits 1, 2, 3; then `fast.next` is None and the loop stops with slow on the middle node, 3.

questions.prompt: This buggy reversal forgets to save `curr.next`. What does it return for the list 1 → 2 → 3?
questions.code:
def reverse(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = curr.next
    return prev
questions.explain: First iteration: `curr.next = prev` sets 1.next to None, then `curr = curr.next` reads that None, so the loop ends after one iteration and returns node 1. Nodes 2 and 3 are lost. It does not loop forever because curr becomes None.

lessons.why: Linked lists teach pointer manipulation, which you'll need for trees, graphs and low-level code, and they're a staple of interviews.

terms.d: Nodes each holding a value and a `next` reference; the list is a reference to the head.
A placeholder node before the real head that removes special cases.
One moves one step, the other two; finds the middle and detects cycles.
Cycle detection where the fast pointer laps the slow one, in O(1) space.

mistakes.wrong: Linked lists are faster than Python lists for everything.
mistakes.right: Indexing a linked list is O(k) from the head. They only win for inserts and deletes next to a node you hold.

mistakes.wrong: I can set `curr.next = prev` and then move on to `curr.next`.
mistakes.right: That loses the rest of the list. Save `nxt = curr.next` first.

takeaways: Save `next` before you overwrite it.
A dummy head simplifies inserts and deletes at the front.
Fast and slow pointers find the middle and detect cycles with O(1) space.

project.title: Build your own hash map
project.brief: Implement a `HashMap` class with separate chaining, automatic resizing and dict-style syntax, then test it against Python's `dict`. Building one yourself is how "O(1) average, O(n) worst case" becomes something you understand rather than memorise.
milestones: Store a list of 8 buckets; implement `put`, `get` and `delete` using `hash(key) % capacity`, raising `KeyError` for missing keys.
Track `size`; when `size / capacity > 0.75`, double the capacity and re-insert every pair. Insert 100,000 keys and check every one can be read back.
Add `__setitem__`, `__getitem__`, `__delitem__`, `__contains__`, `__len__` and `__iter__` so `m[k] = v`, `k in m`, `len(m)` and `for k in m` all work.
Property test: apply 10,000 random put, get and delete operations to your map and to a dict side by side and assert identical results after every step.
Create a key class whose `__hash__` returns 0, time `get` at sizes 1,000 / 2,000 / 4,000, and explain the growth in a comment.
project.stretch: Implement a second version with open addressing and linear probing, using tombstones for deletes, and benchmark it against your chaining version.

exam.prompt: You must check that a string of HTML tags like `` is properly nested. Which data structure fits?
exam.explain: Nesting means the most recently opened tag must close first: last-in, first-out. A queue would match the oldest open tag, and a set loses order and counts.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: "mississippi" has m×1, i×4, s×4, p×2. `counts['s']` is 4 and there are 4 distinct keys: m, i, s, p.

exam.prompt: You group n words of length at most k by using `''.join(sorted(word))` as a dict key. What is the time complexity?
exam.explain: Each word is sorted in O(k log k) and the dict insert is O(k) to hash the key, so n words cost O(n · k log k). Using a 26-letter count tuple as the key instead would make it O(n · k).

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: This evaluates reverse Polish notation. Push 2 and 3; `+` pops both and pushes 5; push 4; `*` pops 4 and 5 and pushes 20. Exactly one value remains.

exam.prompt: You need to detect whether a linked list has a cycle using O(1) extra space. Which technique fits?
options: Store every visited node in a set
Fast and slow pointers: if they ever meet, there is a cycle
exam.explain: Floyd's algorithm uses two pointers and nothing else: O(n) time, O(1) space. The visited set also works but costs O(n) space, which the requirement rules out.

exam.prompt: An LRU cache needs `get` and `put` in O(1), evicting the least recently used key when full. Which combination fits?
options: A hash map from key to node, plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency
A sorted list with binary search
exam.explain: The hash map finds a key's node in O(1), and the doubly linked list moves that node to the front or removes the tail in O(1). A heap needs O(log n) per update, and a sorted list needs O(n) inserts. Python's `OrderedDict` is this exact combination.

lessons.title: Binary search
lessons.objective: By the end you can write a bug-free binary search with a stated invariant, and use bisect to find insertion points and count occurrences.
concept: Binary search finds a target in a **sorted** array by comparing it with the middle element and discarding the half that cannot contain it. Each step halves the range, so it takes **O(log n)** steps: a million elements need at most about 20 comparisons, a billion about 30. The requirement is order, or more generally a yes/no question whose answers switch exactly once from no to yes across the range, so that one comparison tells you which half to keep.

The bugs are almost always off-by-one errors, and the cure is to pick **one interval convention** and keep it. Closed interval `[lo, hi]`: loop `while lo <= hi` and move with `lo = mid + 1` or `hi = mid - 1`. Half-open `[lo, hi)`: start with `hi = len(a)`, loop `while lo < hi`, and move with `lo = mid + 1` or `hi = mid`. Mixing the two causes infinite loops (when `lo = mid` cannot make progress) or skips the answer.

The most useful variant is the **lower bound**: the first index whose value is ≥ x, which is also where x would be inserted to keep the list sorted. `bisect.bisect_left(a, x)` returns it, and `bisect_right` returns the first index whose value is > x. The number of copies of x is `bisect_right(a, x) - bisect_left(a, x)`. Python integers never overflow, so `(lo + hi) // 2` is safe; in Java or C++ write `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`.

example.code:
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right

scores = [10, 20, 20, 20, 35, 50]
print(bisect_left(scores, 20), bisect_right(scores, 20))
print(bisect_right(scores, 20) - bisect_left(scores, 20))
print(bisect_left(scores, 30))
example.explain: The 20s occupy indices 1 to 3, so `bisect_left` gives 1 and `bisect_right` gives 4, and their difference counts the copies: 3. 30 is absent; its insertion point is index 4, just before 35. Output: `1 4`, then `3`, then `4`.

lessons.why: Binary search turns a million-item search into 20 comparisons, and its lower-bound form underpins sorted lookups, databases and many harder problems.

lessons.title: Binary search on the answer
lessons.objective: By the end you can recognise "minimise the maximum" style problems and solve them by binary searching over the range of possible answers with an O(n) feasibility check.
concept: Many optimisation problems hide a binary search where there is no sorted array at all. "What is the minimum eating speed so Koko finishes in h hours?" Define `feasible(v)`: can it be done with speed v? If feasible is **monotonic**, meaning false, false, …, false, true, true, …, true across the possible answers, then the answer is the first true, and you can binary search for it over the range of values rather than over indices.

The recipe has three steps. First, **bound the answer**: `lo` is the smallest conceivable value and `hi` is one that certainly works (for Koko, speed `max(piles)` finishes every pile in one hour). Second, write `feasible(v)`, usually a greedy O(n) pass over the input. Third, run a lower-bound search for the first feasible value. The total cost is **O(n · log R)** where R is the size of the answer range, which is fast even when R is 10^9, since log₂ 10^9 ≈ 30.

Recognise it by phrases like "minimise the maximum", "maximise the minimum", "smallest capacity such that", and by a huge answer range alongside n up to 10^5. The key step is a one-sentence monotonicity argument: if speed k works, any faster speed also works. Ceiling division without floats: `(p + k - 1) // k` or `-(-p // k)`. Floats risk rounding errors when numbers get large, which is a hard bug to spot in an interview.

steps.label: Bound
steps.detail: lo = smallest possible answer, hi = a value that certainly works

steps.label: Feasible
steps.detail: Write feasible(v): usually a greedy O(n) check

steps.label: Probe
steps.detail: mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if feasible(mid): hi = mid, else lo = mid + 1

steps.label: Stop
steps.detail: When lo == hi, it is the first feasible value

steps.label: Cost
steps.detail: O(n · log(hi − lo)) total

example.explain: `hours(k)` is the feasibility check: each pile takes ceil(p / k) hours. Speed 4 needs 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 hours, which fits, while speed 3 needs 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, which does not, so the first feasible speed is 4. Output: `4`.

lessons.title: Merge sort
lessons.objective: By the end you can implement merge sort, explain why it is O(n log n) in every case, and use the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) to analyse divide-and-conquer code.
concept: Merge sort is **divide and conquer**: split the list in half, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves. Merging is the two-pointer technique from Module 1: compare the fronts, take the smaller, advance that pointer, which is O(n). The recursion is log₂ n levels deep, and across each level the merges touch every element once, so the total is **O(n log n)** in the best, average and worst case alike. No input can make it slow.

Merge sort is **stable**: equal elements keep their original relative order, provided the merge takes from the left half on ties (`<=`, not `<`). Stability matters when you sort records by one key after another, such as by name and then by department. The cost is memory: merging needs a buffer, so merge sort uses **O(n) extra space** and is not in place, unlike quicksort or heapsort.

Its running time follows the recurrence **T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)**: two half-size subproblems plus linear combining work, which solves to O(n log n). Learn to read that shape: 2T(n/2) + O(1) is only O(n), and T(n/2) + O(1) is binary search's O(log n). Python's built-in sort is **Timsort**, a merge sort hybrid that is stable, O(n log n) worst case and O(n) on already-sorted data. In real code, call `sorted`; implement merge sort to understand it.

example.code:
def merge_sort(a):
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return a
    mid = len(a) // 2
    left, right = merge_sort(a[:mid]), merge_sort(a[mid:])
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            out.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            out.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    out.extend(left[i:])
    out.extend(right[j:])
    return out

print(merge_sort([5, 2, 9, 1, 5, 6]))
example.explain: The base case is a list of 0 or 1 items, which is already sorted. After both halves come back sorted, the while loop merges them, and whichever half still has items is appended in one go. Using `<=` takes from the left on ties, which keeps the sort stable. Output: `[1, 2, 5, 5, 6, 9]`.

questions.explain: With constant combining work, the recursion tree has about 2n nodes, each doing O(1) work: O(n). O(n log n) needs O(n) work at each level, like merging. O(log n) would require recursing into only one half, as binary search does.

lessons.why: Merge sort is the cleanest example of divide and conquer, and reading its recurrence teaches you to analyse any recursive algorithm.

Combine two sorted lists in O(n) with two pointers.
Equal elements keep their original order.
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n): two half-size subproblems plus linear combining, giving O(n log n).

mistakes.wrong: Merge sort is O(n²) on bad inputs, like quicksort.
mistakes.right: It always splits in half, so it's O(n log n) in every case.

mistakes.wrong: Using `<` or `<=` in the merge makes no difference.

O(n log n) always, at the cost of O(n) extra space.
Learn the recurrence shapes: 2T(n/2)+O(n) is n log n; T(n/2)+O(1) is log n.

lessons.title: Quicksort & partitioning
lessons.objective: By the end you can implement Lomuto partitioning and randomised quicksort, explain its O(n²) worst case, and use partitioning for quickselect.
concept: Quicksort picks a **pivot**, **partitions** the array so that smaller elements come before the pivot and larger ones after it, then recursively sorts each side. Partitioning is a single in-place O(n) pass. If pivots split the array roughly in half, the recursion is about log n deep, giving **O(n log n)** on average with only the recursion stack as extra memory, and in practice it is very fast thanks to tight loops.

The worst case happens when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element, for example always choosing the last element of an already-sorted array. Every split is then sizes n − 1 and 0: **O(n²)** time and recursion depth n, enough to hit Python's recursion limit. Choosing a **random pivot** makes the expected time O(n log n) on every input. Quicksort is **not stable**, because swaps carry elements past their equals.

**Lomuto partition**: take `pivot = a[hi]` and let `i` mark the end of the "less than pivot" region. Scan `j` from `lo` to `hi - 1`; whenever `a[j] < pivot`, swap it into position i and advance i. Finally swap the pivot into `a[i]`, its final sorted position. Partitioning on its own powers **quickselect**: to find the k-th smallest element, recurse into only the side that contains index k, for **O(n) average**. A three-way variant (the Dutch national flag) handles many duplicates.

steps.label: j = 0
steps.detail: 7 ≥ 5: skip. i stays 0

steps.label: j = 2
steps.detail: 9 ≥ 5: skip

steps.label: Place pivot
steps.detail: swap a[2], a[4] → [2, 4, 5, 7, 9]; pivot index 2 is final

example.code:
import random

def partition(a, lo, hi):
    pivot = a[hi]
    i = lo
    for j in range(lo, hi):
        if a[j] < pivot:
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
            i += 1
    a[i], a[hi] = a[hi], a[i]
    return i

def quicksort(a, lo=0, hi=None):
    if hi is None:
        hi = len(a) - 1
    if lo < hi:
        r = random.randint(lo, hi)
        a[r], a[hi] = a[hi], a[r]
        p = partition(a, lo, hi)
        quicksort(a, lo, p - 1)
        quicksort(a, p + 1, hi)

nums = [7, 2, 9, 4, 5, 1]
quicksort(nums)
print(nums)
example.explain: Before partitioning, a random element is swapped into the pivot slot, so no fixed input pattern can force bad splits. After `partition`, index p holds its final value and the two sides are sorted independently. The sort happens in place. Output: `[1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9]`.

questions.explain: Each round partitions and keeps one side, so on average the work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≈ 2n = O(n). Sorting first would be O(n log n). The worst case, with consistently bad pivots, is still O(n²).

questions.prompt: You must sort 10 million order records by date, and orders with the same date must keep their existing order. Which algorithm meets the requirement?
options: Merge sort (or Python's sorted, which is a stable Timsort)

Rearrange so smaller elements come before the pivot and larger after, in one O(n) pass.
Pivot is the last element; `i` marks the end of the smaller region.

mistakes.right: Bad pivots (always the smallest or largest) give O(n²). A random pivot makes that vanishingly unlikely.

lessons.title: Sorting as a tool
lessons.objective: By the end you can spot when sorting first simplifies a problem, and write multi-key sorts with key functions.
concept: Sorting first often turns a hard problem into an easy one for O(n log n). After sorting, duplicates sit next to each other, two pointers work (3Sum becomes sort plus an O(n) two-pointer scan per element), overlapping intervals can be merged in one sweep, and greedy choices become obvious. With n up to 10^5, an extra O(n log n) step is almost always affordable, so "would this be easier if the input were sorted?" is a question worth asking early.

Python gives you two tools. `sorted(iterable)` returns a new list; `a.sort()` sorts in place and **returns None**, so `x = a.sort()` is a classic bug. The `key=` argument maps each element to what should be compared: `key=len`, or `key=lambda p: (p.age, p.name)`. Tuples compare element by element, so one tuple key gives a multi-level sort. Use `reverse=True` for descending order, and negate numbers to mix directions: `key=lambda r: (-r.score, r.name)`.

**Merge intervals**: sort by start, then walk through the intervals. If the current one starts at or before the end of the last merged interval, extend that end with `max`; otherwise begin a new interval. One sort plus one pass is O(n log n). When keys are small integers, such as ages from 0 to 120, **counting sort** places items into buckets in O(n + k) time and beats any comparison sort, whose lower bound is O(n log n).

steps.detail: merged = [[1,3]]
2 ≤ 3 overlaps: extend end to max(3, 6) → [[1,6]]

modules.summary: Traverse trees recursively and iteratively, use BST ordering, and reach for heaps and tries when a problem asks for the best k or for prefix lookups.

lessons.title: Binary trees & traversals
lessons.objective: By the end you can write preorder, inorder, postorder and level-order traversals recursively and iteratively, and solve tree problems by combining answers from the children.
concept: A binary tree node holds a value and up to two children, `left` and `right`. The three depth-first traversals differ only in **when the node itself is visited**: preorder visits the node, then left, then right; inorder visits left, node, right; postorder visits left, right, node. **Level order** (breadth-first) visits row by row with a queue. All of them are **O(n)** time. Recursive versions use **O(h)** stack space, where h is the height: O(log n) for a balanced tree and O(n) for a chain.

Most tree problems follow one pattern: **solve for the children, then combine at the node**. Maximum depth is `1 + max(depth(left), depth(right))` with `depth(None) = 0`. Before writing the code, decide in one sentence what your function returns for a subtree, and what it returns for `None`. Then trust the recursive call to do its job; tracing every level in your head is unnecessary and error-prone.

Iterative traversals replace the call stack with your own stack. **Preorder**: pop a node, visit it, then push its right child before its left so the left is processed first. **Inorder**: walk left as far as possible pushing every node, pop one and visit it, then move to its right child and repeat. The iterative versions avoid Python's recursion limit on very deep trees (10^4 or more levels), and interviewers often ask for them as a follow-up.

lessons.title: Binary search trees
lessons.objective: By the end you can insert into, search and validate a BST, and explain why its operations are O(h) and when h becomes n.
concept: A **binary search tree** keeps one invariant: every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node, and every value in its right subtree is larger. The rule covers whole subtrees, not just direct children. Search, insert and delete each walk a single root-to-leaf path, comparing at each node to decide which way to go, so they cost **O(h)**. In a balanced tree h ≈ log₂ n; insert already-sorted values and the tree degenerates into a chain with h = n.

An **inorder traversal of a BST yields its values in sorted order**. That gives you quick solutions to "k-th smallest" (stop after k visits) and "is this a valid BST?" (check that the inorder sequence is strictly increasing). The classic validation bug compares each node only with its children. Instead pass down an allowed range `(low, high)`: going left tightens `high` to the node's value, and going right tightens `low`.

**Self-balancing** trees such as AVL and red-black trees perform rotations on insert and delete to keep h = O(log n); they power Java's `TreeMap` and C++'s `std::map`. Python has no balanced BST in the standard library. In practice you use a sorted list with `bisect` (O(log n) search, O(n) insert, fast for moderate n), the third-party `sortedcontainers.SortedList`, or a heap when you only ever need the minimum or maximum.

Search, insert and delete walk one path, so cost depends on height.

AVL or red-black trees rotate to keep h = O(log n).

mistakes.right: The rule covers whole subtrees. Pass down min and max bounds, or check that inorder is strictly increasing.

mistakes.right: Only when the tree is balanced. Sorted inserts make it O(n).

lessons.title: Heaps & priority queues
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain how a binary heap stored in a list supports O(log n) push and pop, and use heapq for min-heaps, max-heaps and prioritised tasks.
concept: A binary **min-heap** is a complete binary tree in which every parent is ≤ its children, so the smallest element is always at the root. Because the tree is complete, it fits in a plain list with no pointers: the children of index i are at `2i + 1` and `2i + 2`, and its parent is at `(i - 1) // 2`. A heap is only partially ordered: siblings and cousins can be in any order, which is what makes it cheaper to maintain than a sorted list.

**Push** appends the new item at the end, then sifts it up, swapping with its parent while it is smaller: O(log n). **Pop** removes the root, moves the last item to the root, then sifts it down, swapping with the smaller child: O(log n). Peeking at the minimum is `h[0]`, O(1). **Heapify** turns an arbitrary list into a heap in O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes sit near the bottom and only sift a short distance.

Python's `heapq` module works on a regular list and is **min-heap only**: `heappush`, `heappop`, `heapify`, `heapreplace`, `nsmallest`, `nlargest`. For a max-heap, push negated numbers and negate again when you pop. For prioritised items, push tuples `(priority, counter, item)`: tuples compare element by element, and the unique counter breaks ties so Python never has to compare the items themselves, which may not support `<`.

example.code:
import heapq

tasks = []
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, "write tests"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (1, "fix prod bug"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (3, "refactor"))
print(heapq.heappop(tasks)[1])

max_heap = [-x for x in [5, 1, 8, 3, 9]]
heapq.heapify(max_heap)
print(-heapq.heappop(max_heap))
example.explain: Tuples compare by their first element, so the lowest priority number pops first. For the max-heap, each value is stored negated, so the largest original value becomes the smallest stored one. Output: `fix prod bug`, then `9`.

questions.explain: With the root at index 0, the children of i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and the parent of i is (i − 1) // 2. The formulas 2i and 2i + 1 apply only when the root is stored at index 1.

questions.explain: Bottom-up heapify sifts each node down only as far as its height, and most nodes are near the leaves, so the total is O(n). Pushing the items one at a time would be O(n log n).

h = []
heapq.heappush(h, (1, {"id": "a"}))
heapq.heappush(h, (1, {"id": "b"}))

The second item replaces the first
questions.explain: With equal priorities, tuple comparison moves to the second element, and dicts do not support `<`, so `heappush` raises TypeError. Push `(priority, next(counter), item)` so ties are broken by a unique integer.

lessons.why: Whenever you need 'the next most urgent thing' (schedulers, Dijkstra, merging streams), a heap gives it to you in O(log n) instead of re-sorting.

Children of index i live at 2i+1 and 2i+2; no pointers needed.
Swap a new or moved item with its parent or smaller child until the order holds.
Turn a list into a heap in O(n).

mistakes.wrong: A heap keeps the whole list sorted.
mistakes.right: Only the root is guaranteed to be the minimum; the rest is only partially ordered.

mistakes.wrong: `heapq` has a max-heap mode.
mistakes.right: It's min-heap only. Push negated values (or `(-priority, item)`) for a max-heap.

takeaways: Push and pop are O(log n); peeking at the minimum is O(1).
Tuples like `(priority, counter, task)` order tasks and break ties.
`heapify` builds a heap from a list in linear time.

lessons.title: Top-k problems
lessons.objective: By the end you can choose between sorting, a size-k heap, quickselect and bucketing for top-k problems, and solve streaming median with two heaps.
concept: "The k largest", "the k most frequent", "the k closest points": these are top-k problems, and the go-to tool is a **heap of size k**. For the k largest, keep a min-heap of the best k seen so far. For each new x, push it, and if the heap now holds more than k items, pop the smallest. The root is always the k-th largest so far. Time **O(n log k)**, space **O(k)**: excellent when k is much smaller than n or when the data arrives as a stream.

There are alternatives. Sorting is O(n log n) and the simplest code, which is fine when n is small. Quickselect is O(n) on average but mutates the input and is O(n²) in the worst case. For "top k frequent", **bucket sort by count** is O(n) because no count can exceed n. `heapq.nlargest(k, iterable, key=...)` builds the size-k heap for you, so use it rather than writing the loop by hand.

**Running median** uses two heaps: a max-heap (negated values) for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, with sizes kept within one of each other. Each insert is O(log n) and the median is read from one or both tops in O(1). **K-way merge** of k sorted lists pushes the head of each list, pops the smallest, then pushes that list's next element: O(N log k) for N total items. That is how databases merge sorted runs on disk.

example.explain: `nlargest` iterates over the Counter's keys and ranks them by `counts.get`, their frequency. In `kth_largest`, the heap never holds more than k items, and after the scan its root is the 2nd largest value, 5. Output: `[1, 2] 5`.

questions.explain: The min-heap's root is the weakest of the current top k, so it is the one to compare with and evict. A max-heap of size k would put the largest at the root, which is the wrong item to evict. Heaps of all items cost O(n) space.

print(heapq.nlargest(2, ["apple", "fig", "banana", "kiwi"], key=len))

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of finding the k largest of n numbers with a size-k heap?
questions.explain: Each of the n items costs at most one push and one pop on a heap that never exceeds k + 1 items, so O(log k) each: O(n log k) in total.

questions.prompt: You must report the median after every number in a stream of 10^6 numbers. Which data structure fits?
options: A max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half
A sorted list, re-sorted after every insert
questions.explain: Two heaps give O(log n) inserts and O(1) median reads. Re-sorting after each insert costs at least O(n) every time, about 10^12 work in total. A single heap only exposes one extreme, and a set has no order.

O(n) average for the k-th element, but mutates the input.
