lessons.title: Tries
lessons.objective: By the end you can implement a trie with insert, search and prefix queries, and explain when it beats a hash set.
concept: A **trie** (prefix tree) stores strings one character per level. Each node holds a dict of children and a flag marking that a word ends there. Words with a common prefix share the same path, so "car", "cat" and "cart" share the nodes for c and a. Inserting or looking up a word of length L costs **O(L)**, independent of how many words are stored. That is the same cost as hashing a string of length L.

The trie's real advantage is **prefix queries**. "Does any word start with `auto`?" is a walk of 4 nodes. "List every word starting with `auto`" walks to that node, then runs a DFS below it to collect completions. A hash set answers exact membership just as fast, but for prefix questions it must scan every stored word. That is why tries back autocomplete, spell checkers, and word search on a grid, where a DFS can stop as soon as its path is not the prefix of any word.

The cost is **memory**: one node per distinct prefix, each with its own dict, which can be many times larger than the raw strings. You can store extra data on nodes to make queries faster, such as a count of words passing through ("how many words start with `pre`?") or a cached list of the top suggestions. A compact implementation uses nested dicts with a sentinel key such as `"$"` to mark the end of a word.

questions.explain: The search follows at most L edges, one per character, and never looks at other words, so N does not appear. Scanning a list of words would be O(L · N).

questions.prompt: A search box must suggest completions for each prefix a user types, over a dictionary of 10^6 words. Which data structure fits best?

A heap orders by a single key and a queue by insertion; neither groups words by prefix. (A sorted list with `bisect` is another valid option, but it is not among the choices.)

lessons.why: Autocomplete, spell-checkers and routing tables all ask prefix questions. A trie answers them in time proportional to the prefix, not the number of words.

terms.d: A tree storing strings one character per level, sharing common prefixes.
Marks that a complete word ends at a node.
Walk the prefix's characters, then explore below that node.
Insert and search cost the length of the word, not the number of words.

mistakes.right: It may only be a prefix of a longer word. Check the end-of-word flag.

mistakes.wrong: A trie always uses less memory than a set of strings.
mistakes.right: Each node has its own dict, so a trie can be many times larger. It wins on prefix queries, not space.

Insert and search are O(L).
Store extra data on nodes (counts, top words) to speed up queries.

import heapq
lists = [[1, 4, 9], [2, 3], [5]]

heapq.heapify(heap)

modules.title: Graphs
modules.summary: Model problems as graphs and pick the right traversal: BFS for unweighted shortest paths, DFS and union-find for connectivity, Kahn's for dependencies, and Dijkstra for weighted shortest paths.

lessons.title: Graph representations
lessons.objective: By the end you can model a problem as a graph, build an adjacency list from an edge list, and choose between adjacency list, matrix and edge list by their costs.
concept: A graph is a set of **vertices** joined by **edges**. Edges can be directed (follows, prerequisite of) or undirected (friendship, a road), and weighted (distance, price) or unweighted. Many problems are graphs in disguise: grid cells whose neighbours are up, down, left and right; words that differ by one letter (Word Ladder); courses and their prerequisites; package dependencies. The first skill is spotting the vertices and edges in a problem statement that never uses the word "graph".

The default representation is an **adjacency list**: a dict mapping each vertex to a list of its neighbours, or to `(neighbour, weight)` pairs. It uses O(V + E) space, and iterating over the neighbours of u costs O(deg(u)). An **adjacency matrix** is a V × V grid where `m[u][v]` holds 1 or the weight. Checking one edge is O(1), but it costs O(V²) space and O(V) to list neighbours, so use it only for small or dense graphs. An **edge list** of `(u, v, w)` tuples is a common input format and is what union-find and Kruskal consume.

Build an adjacency list from an edge list with `defaultdict(list)`. For an **undirected** graph add both directions; forgetting the reverse edge is one of the most common graph bugs. For grids, do not build a graph at all: compute neighbours on the fly with direction offsets and a bounds check. An undirected graph has at most V(V − 1)/2 edges, so a graph is called **dense** when E is close to V² and **sparse** when E is close to V.

example.explain: Each undirected edge is added in both directions, so d lists b and c. The grid helper never stores a graph; it generates in-bounds neighbours on demand, and a corner cell has only two. Output: `['b', 'c'] [(1, 0), (0, 1)]`.

lessons.tryit: For each of these, write down on paper what the vertices and edges are, whether edges are directed or weighted, and which representation you would use: (1) Word Ladder from "hit" to "cog", (2) a 1000 × 1000 maze, (3) flights between 300 airports with prices, (4) course prerequisites. Then write `build_graph(edges, directed)` and test it on one directed and one undirected edge list.

questions.prompt: How much space does an adjacency matrix use for a graph with V vertices and E edges?
questions.explain: The matrix has a cell for every ordered pair of vertices, whether or not an edge exists: V × V. O(V + E) is the adjacency list's cost.

questions.prompt: A 100 × 100 grid allows moves up, down, left and right between adjacent cells. How many vertices and undirected edges does it have?
questions.explain: Each of the 100 rows has 99 horizontal edges (9,900) and each of the 100 columns has 99 vertical edges (9,900): 19,800 in total. 40,000 counts each cell's four directions without removing the borders and the double counting.

questions.prompt: A social network has 10^6 users with about 200 friends each. Which representation should you use?
options: An adjacency list (or dict of sets)
An edge list scanned for every query
A single sorted list of user ids
questions.explain: The graph is sparse: about 10^8 adjacency entries in a list, versus 10^12 cells in a matrix, far beyond memory. An edge list makes every neighbour query O(E). A dict of sets also adds O(1) "are they friends?" checks.

lessons.why: Maps, networks, dependencies and social connections are graphs. Spotting the graph and choosing a representation is usually the hardest part of the problem.

A dict from each vertex to its neighbours: O(V + E) space.
A V × V grid: O(1) edge checks but O(V²) space.
Few edges compared with V² / close to V² edges.

mistakes.right: Add both directions, or traversals will miss half the edges.

mistakes.right: Generate neighbours on the fly with direction offsets; the grid already is the graph.

Use a matrix only for dense graphs or constant-time edge checks.
Many problems become graphs: states as vertices, moves as edges.

lessons.title: Breadth-first search
lessons.objective: By the end you can use BFS to find shortest paths in unweighted graphs and grids, reconstruct the path, and run multi-source BFS.
concept: BFS explores a graph in rings: first every vertex at distance 1 from the start, then every vertex at distance 2, and so on, driven by a FIFO queue (`deque`). Because of that order, the **first time BFS reaches a vertex, it has found a shortest path** to it in an unweighted graph, meaning the fewest edges. Each vertex is enqueued once and each edge examined once (twice if undirected), so BFS runs in **O(V + E)**.

Mark a vertex as visited **when you enqueue it**, not when you dequeue it. If you wait until dequeue, the same vertex can be added to the queue many times by different neighbours, wasting time and memory. A `dist` dict does both jobs: membership means visited, and the value is the distance. To recover the path itself, store `parent[v] = u` when you discover v, then walk the parents back from the target and reverse.

**Multi-source BFS** starts with several vertices in the queue at distance 0. It answers "distance to the nearest exit" or "minutes until every orange rots" in one pass. When the answer is a number of levels, process one level at a time with `for _ in range(len(q))`. The state does not have to be a plain vertex: it can be `(row, col, keys_held)`. If edges have different weights, BFS no longer gives shortest paths; that is Dijkstra's job.

steps.detail: queue [A], dist {A: 0}

steps.label: Pop A
steps.detail: discover B and C at distance 1 → queue [B, C]

steps.label: Pop B
steps.detail: discover D at distance 2 → queue [C, D]

steps.label: Pop C

steps.label: Pop D

questions.prompt: Which data structure drives BFS?
questions.explain: BFS must process vertices in the order they were discovered, which is first-in, first-out. A stack gives DFS and a min-heap gives Dijkstra. A set records visits but imposes no order.

questions.prompt: Which problem is solved directly by BFS?
options: The minimum number of moves for a knight to go from one square to another
The cheapest flight route when every flight has a different price
Finding the maximum value in a binary tree
questions.explain: Every knight move costs the same, so the fewest moves is a shortest path in an unweighted graph: BFS. Different prices make the graph weighted, which needs Dijkstra.

questions.prompt: Why should BFS mark a vertex visited when it is enqueued rather than when it is dequeued?
options: Otherwise the same vertex can be enqueued many times before it is processed, wasting time and memory
Otherwise the distances come out wrong
questions.explain: With dequeue-time marking, every neighbour that discovers v before v is processed adds another copy, which can blow up on dense graphs or open grids. The first copy is still popped first, so distances stay correct; the cost is wasted work.

lessons.why: BFS gives shortest paths whenever every step costs the same: mazes, word ladders, fewest moves, degrees of separation.

The first time BFS reaches a vertex, it has the fewest edges.
Record where each vertex was reached from to rebuild the path.
Start with several vertices at distance 0 to find nearest distances in one pass.

mistakes.wrong: Mark vertices visited when I take them off the queue.
mistakes.right: Mark them when you enqueue; otherwise the same vertex can be queued many times.

mistakes.wrong: BFS finds the cheapest path when edges have weights.
mistakes.right: It minimises edge count only. Weighted graphs need Dijkstra.

Mark visited on enqueue.
Keep a parent map if you need the path, not just its length.

lessons.title: DFS, connected components & union-find
lessons.objective: By the end you can count connected components with DFS, implement union-find with path compression and union by size, and say when each fits.
concept: DFS goes as deep as possible before backtracking, using recursion or an explicit stack, in **O(V + E)**. It does not find shortest paths, but it is the tool for "explore everything reachable": flood fill, cycle detection, topological sort and backtracking. **Connected components**: loop over every vertex, and each time you find an unvisited one, start a DFS from it and add 1 to the count. Number of Islands is exactly this on a grid, with land cells as vertices.

Watch the recursion depth. An all-land 100 × 100 grid makes recursive DFS 10,000 calls deep, far past Python's default limit of 1,000, and it raises `RecursionError`. Use an explicit stack (or BFS) for big inputs. Mark a cell visited when you push it, either in a `seen` set or by overwriting the grid cell if you are allowed to mutate it, so it is never pushed twice.

**Union-find** (disjoint set union) answers "are a and b connected?" while edges arrive one at a time, with no need to re-run a DFS after each one. A `parent` array points every element toward its set's root. `find(x)` follows parents up to the root; `union(a, b)` links one root under the other. With **path compression** (repointing nodes closer to the root during find) and **union by size** (attaching the smaller tree under the larger), each operation is amortized O(α(n)), where α is so slow-growing it is at most 4 for any practical n.

Use union-find for counting components as edges stream in, detecting a cycle in an undirected graph (union of two elements that already share a root), Kruskal's minimum spanning tree (sort edges by weight and keep each edge that joins two different sets), and problems like Redundant Connection or Accounts Merge. Its limits: it cannot delete edges, and it tells you whether two elements are connected but not the path between them. For a path, use BFS or DFS.

left.title: DFS / BFS
points: Needs the whole graph up front
Gives component members and actual paths
Re-run after every new edge: expensive

right.title: Union-find
points: Processes edges one at a time
Near-O(1) amortized per union or find
Answers same-set queries and counts components

example.explain: `find` uses path halving, a simple form of path compression: each step points a node at its grandparent. `union` attaches the smaller tree under the larger and returns False when both elements already share a root, which means the edge closes a cycle. Output: `cycle via (2, 0)`, then `2 True`.

Test both on a 200 × 200 all-land grid. Then use the DSU to solve LeetCode 684 (Redundant Connection).

options: The root (representative) of the set containing x
The number of elements in x's set
The shortest path from x to the root
questions.explain: Two elements are in the same set exactly when their finds return the same root. Set sizes are tracked separately (in `size`), and union-find never produces paths.

questions.prompt: What does this print?

return 1 + area(grid, r + 1, c) + area(grid, r - 1, c) + area(grid, r, c + 1) + area(grid, r, c - 1)
questions.explain: Check bounds and water first, then sink the cell before recursing. If the recursive calls came before `grid[r][c] = 0`, neighbours would recurse back into this cell forever.

questions.prompt: Network links are added one at a time, and after each addition you must report the number of connected components. Which approach fits?
options: Run a full DFS after every new link
Union-find, decrementing a counter on every successful union
BFS from vertex 0 after every link
Sort the links by vertex id
questions.explain: Each union is near-O(1), so E additions cost about O(E α(V)). Re-running DFS costs O(V + E) per addition, O(E·(V + E)) in total. BFS from one vertex only finds that vertex's component.

lessons.why: 'Which things are connected?' is a basic question in networks, images and clustering. DFS answers it once; union-find answers it as connections keep arriving.

terms.d: Go as deep as possible before backtracking, recursively or with a stack.
A maximal set of vertices that can all reach each other.
Tracks which set each element belongs to, merging sets as edges arrive.
Optimisations that keep union-find operations nearly O(1).

mistakes.wrong: Recursive DFS is fine on any grid.
mistakes.right: A 100 × 100 all-land grid recurses 10,000 deep and hits Python's limit. Use an explicit stack.

mistakes.wrong: DFS gives shortest paths too.
mistakes.right: DFS finds reachability, not distances. Use BFS for fewest steps.

takeaways: Count components by starting a DFS from each unvisited vertex.
Use union-find when edges stream in or for cycle detection and Kruskal's MST.
Path compression and union by size make union-find nearly constant time.

lessons.title: Topological sort
lessons.objective: By the end you can produce a topological order with Kahn's algorithm, detect a cycle from its output, and explain the DFS-based alternative.
concept: A **topological order** of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) lists every vertex so that each edge u → v has u before v. It models dependencies: courses and prerequisites, build systems such as make, package installation order, spreadsheet recalculation. If the graph contains a cycle, no such order exists, because the vertices on the cycle each have to come before one another. Detecting that cycle ("circular dependency") is often half the problem.

**Kahn's algorithm** is BFS on in-degrees. Count each vertex's incoming edges. Put every vertex with in-degree 0 in a queue: these have no unmet dependencies. Pop u, append it to the order, and decrement the in-degree of each neighbour, enqueueing any neighbour that reaches 0. If the final order contains fewer than V vertices, the rest are stuck on a cycle. The whole process is **O(V + E)**.

The **DFS version** appends each vertex after all its descendants have finished (postorder), then reverses the list. Topological orders are usually **not unique**, and any valid one is accepted unless the problem asks for something specific; for the lexicographically smallest order, use a min-heap instead of a queue in Kahn's. LeetCode 207 and 210 (Course Schedule I and II) are this exact algorithm with the edge direction prerequisite → course.

visual.title: Kahn's algorithm on a→b, a→c, b→d, c→d

steps.label: In-degrees
steps.detail: a 0, b 1, c 1, d 2 → queue [a]

steps.label: Pop a
steps.detail: order [a]; b and c drop to 0 → queue [b, c]

steps.label: Pop b
steps.detail: order [a, b]; d drops to 1

steps.label: Pop c
steps.detail: order [a, b, c]; d drops to 0 → queue [d]

steps.label: Pop d
steps.detail: order [a, b, c, d]: all 4 vertices placed, so there is no cycle

example.code:
from collections import deque, defaultdict

def course_order(n, prereqs):
    graph = defaultdict(list)
    indeg = [0] * n
    for course, pre in prereqs:
        graph[pre].append(course)
        indeg[course] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0)
    order = []
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        order.append(u)
        for v in graph[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0:
                q.append(v)
    return order if len(order) == n else []

print(course_order(4, [[1, 0], [2, 0], [3, 1], [3, 2]]))
print(course_order(2, [[0, 1], [1, 0]]))
example.explain: Each pair `[course, pre]` becomes an edge pre → course. Course 0 has no prerequisites, so it goes first, which unlocks 1 and 2, which together unlock 3. In the second call, 0 and 1 require each other, nothing ever reaches in-degree 0, and the empty list signals the cycle. Output: `[0, 1, 2, 3]`, then `[]`.

Only when every vertex has in-degree at most 1
questions.explain: A cycle makes "u before v" contradictory for the vertices on it, and every DAG has at least one valid order. Connectivity does not matter: independent pieces can be interleaved freely.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of Kahn's algorithm?

The 2 missing vertices have no edges

A list where every edge u → v has u before v.
The number of edges coming into a vertex: its unmet dependencies.
Repeatedly take vertices with in-degree 0 and decrement their neighbours.

lessons.title: Dijkstra's algorithm
lessons.objective: By the end you can implement Dijkstra with heapq and lazy deletion, explain why it needs non-negative weights, and describe how A* extends it.
concept: With weighted edges, fewest edges is not cheapest: a single edge of weight 10 loses to three edges of weight 1. **Dijkstra's algorithm** generalises BFS by replacing the FIFO queue with a **min-heap keyed on distance so far**, so it always expands the closest vertex that is not yet finished. It requires every edge weight to be **non-negative**, and it computes the cheapest distance from the source to every reachable vertex in one run.

With **lazy deletion**: start with `dist = {src: 0}` and `heap = [(0, src)]`. Pop `(d, u)`; if `d > dist[u]`, the entry is stale, because a shorter path was already found, so skip it. Otherwise **relax** every edge u → v of weight w: if `d + w` beats `dist.get(v, inf)`, update `dist[v]` and push `(d + w, v)`. `heapq` has no decrease-key operation, which is why duplicates are pushed and filtered on pop. With a binary heap the cost is **O((V + E) log V)**.

Why non-negative? When u is popped with the smallest tentative distance d, any other route to u must leave the finished region through some vertex whose distance is already ≥ d, then add non-negative weights, so it cannot be shorter. A negative edge breaks that argument; use **Bellman–Ford** (O(V·E)) instead. A* is Dijkstra with priority `d + h(v)`, where h is an admissible heuristic that never overestimates the remaining cost, such as Manhattan distance on a 4-direction grid. It finds the same answer while exploring fewer vertices.

visual.title: Dijkstra from A: A→B 4, A→C 1, C→B 2, B→D 1, C→D 5

example.explain: This is the run shown in the table. The direct edge A→B (4) is beaten by A→C→B (3), and that improvement then makes D reachable for 4 instead of 6. The stale heap entries (4, B) and (6, D) are popped and ignored. Output: `{'A': 0, 'B': 3, 'C': 1, 'D': 4}`.

questions.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm replaces BFS's FIFO queue with which data structure?
options: A min-heap (priority queue) keyed on distance
A max-heap keyed on edge weight
A sorted list of vertices by id
questions.explain: Dijkstra always expands the unfinished vertex with the smallest known distance, which is exactly what a min-heap provides in O(log n). A stack would give DFS order.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: S→B costs 2, B→A brings A down from 5 to 3, and A→T gives 4, beating both S→A→T (6) and S→B→T (9). The cheapest route uses the most edges, which is why BFS would get this wrong.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra with a binary heap on V vertices and E edges?
questions.explain: Every edge can cause one push, and each push or pop costs O(log V) (log E is within a constant factor of log V). O(V + E) is BFS; O(V · E) is Bellman–Ford.

questions.prompt: A graph has one edge of weight −3. What can go wrong with Dijkstra?
options: A vertex can be finalised too early, before a cheaper path through the negative edge is found, so it returns a wrong distance
It raises an error on negative numbers
questions.explain: The correctness argument assumes that leaving the finished region can only add cost. A negative edge can make a path through a far-away vertex cheaper after a closer vertex was already popped. Python raises no error; you silently get a wrong answer. Use Bellman–Ford for negative weights.

lessons.why: Route planners, network routing and game AI need cheapest paths when steps cost different amounts. Dijkstra is the standard tool.

terms.d: If going through u gives v a shorter distance, update it and push v.
Always expand the closest unfinished vertex next.
Skip heap entries whose distance is larger than the best known.
Dijkstra plus a heuristic estimate of the remaining distance, to search toward the goal.

mistakes.wrong: Dijkstra works with negative edge weights if I'm careful.
mistakes.right: A negative edge can make a finished vertex's distance wrong. Use Bellman–Ford for negative weights.

mistakes.wrong: I must update entries inside the heap when a distance improves.
mistakes.right: Push a new entry and skip stale ones when popped; that's simpler and just as fast in practice.

takeaways: BFS with a min-heap instead of a queue.
Requires non-negative weights.
O((V + E) log V) with `heapq` and lazy deletion.

exam.code:
from collections import deque
grid = [[2, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0], [0, 1, 1]]
q = deque((r, c, 0) for r in range(3) for c in range(3) if grid[r][c] == 2)
minutes = 0
while q:
    r, c, t = q.popleft()
    minutes = max(minutes, t)
    for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
        if 0 <= nr < 3 and 0 <= nc < 3 and grid[nr][nc] == 1:
            grid[nr][nc] = 2
            q.append((nr, nc, t + 1))
print(minutes)
exam.explain: Rot spreads one ring per minute from (0,0): minute 1 reaches (0,1) and (1,0); minute 2 reaches (0,2) and (1,1); minute 3 reaches (2,1); minute 4 reaches (2,2). (1,2) is empty, so (2,2) can only be reached from (2,1).

exam.prompt: To detect a cycle in a directed graph, a student runs DFS and reports a cycle whenever it reaches an already-visited vertex. On the graph A→B, A→C, B→D, C→D, what happens?
options: It wrongly reports a cycle, because D is reached a second time via C even though no cycle exists
exam.explain: Reaching a finished vertex again is normal in a DAG; the diamond is acyclic. A directed cycle exists only if DFS reaches a vertex that is still on the current path ("in progress"). That is why directed cycle detection uses three states, or Kahn's algorithm.

exam.prompt: With path compression and union by size, what is the amortized cost of a union-find operation?
exam.explain: Together the two optimisations give the inverse-Ackermann bound α(n), which is at most 4 for any realistic n. With union by size alone, the bound is O(log n); with neither, a chain can make finds O(n).

exam.prompt: A package manager must install packages so that each one's dependencies are installed first, and refuse when dependencies are circular. Which algorithm fits?
options: Topological sort (Kahn's), reporting a cycle when not every package is output
BFS on the undirected version of the graph
exam.explain: "Dependencies first" is precisely a topological order, and Kahn's algorithm detects cycles for free when its output is short. Dijkstra and BFS compute distances, not dependency orders, and treating the graph as undirected discards the direction that matters.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: The unions merge {0, 1}, {2, 3}, then both into {0, 1, 2, 3} through the (1, 3) union, plus {4, 5}. Two distinct roots remain. This version has no path compression, which affects speed but not correctness.

exam.prompt: Why does the `heapq` version of Dijkstra push duplicate entries for a vertex and skip stale ones when popped?
options: `heapq` has no decrease-key operation, so pushing a new, smaller entry and ignoring outdated ones is the simplest way to update a priority
Duplicates make the algorithm run faster
It is needed to handle negative weights
exam.explain: A binary heap stored in a list can't find an arbitrary entry efficiently, so the outdated entry is left in place and filtered out on pop. The heap grows to O(E) entries, so the cost is still O((V + E) log V). It does nothing to make negative weights work.

exam.prompt: Word Ladder asks for the fewest one-letter changes that turn "hit" into "cog", using only dictionary words. Which algorithm fits?
options: BFS over words, where words that differ by one letter are neighbours
exam.explain: Each change costs the same, so the fewest changes is a shortest path in an unweighted graph: BFS. Union-find could tell you that "cog" is reachable, but not how many steps it takes.

modules.title: DP, greedy, backtracking & problem-solving method
modules.summary: Turn recursion into DP tables, know when greedy is provably right, generate search spaces with backtracking, and solve unseen problems with a repeatable process.

lessons.title: Recursion → memoization → tabulation (1D DP)
lessons.objective: By the end you can turn a recursive solution into a memoized one, then a bottom-up table, then an O(1)-space loop, and apply that sequence to house robber and coin change.
concept: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has **overlapping subproblems** (the same smaller question is asked many times) and **optimal substructure** (the best answer is built from best answers to smaller questions). Naive recursive Fibonacci shows the waste: `fib(n)` calls `fib(n-1)` and `fib(n-2)`, and both of those call `fib(n-3)`, and so on. The call tree grows like φ^n ≈ 1.6^n, so `fib(40)` makes over 300 million calls.

The sequence is mechanical once you have a recurrence. **1. Recurse**: write the recursive solution with a clearly defined state, such as "`ways(i)` = number of ways to reach step i". **2. Memoize**: cache each state's answer with `@functools.cache` or a dict, so each state is computed once: O(states × work per state). **3. Tabulate**: fill an array from the base cases upward in dependency order, with no recursion and so no recursion limit. **4. Compress**: if each state reads only the last one or two, keep just those variables for O(1) space.

**House robber**: you cannot rob two adjacent houses, so `best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + nums[i])`, meaning skip house i or rob it. **Coin change** (fewest coins): `best(a) = 1 + min(best(a - c))` over coins c ≤ a, with `best(0) = 0`, in O(amount × coins). The hard part is always the state definition and the recurrence, and once you write those down in words, the code follows. If a recurrence needs more than one changing parameter, the table becomes 2D, which is the next lesson.

visual.title: Four forms of the same solution

steps.label: Memoized
steps.detail: same code plus a cache: O(n) time, O(n) space (cache and stack)

Then solve LeetCode 322 (Coin Change) top-down with `@cache` and bottom-up with a list, returning -1 when the amount cannot be made.

questions.prompt: Which two properties tell you a problem can be solved with dynamic programming?
options: Sorted input and a monotonic predicate
A greedy choice and a stack
questions.explain: DP saves work by reusing answers to repeated subproblems, and the answers must combine into an optimal whole. A monotonic predicate is the signature of binary search; non-negative weights are Dijkstra's requirement.

for i in range(2, n + 1):
    dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2]
print(dp[n])

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of memoized coin change for amount A and k coin types?
questions.explain: There are A + 1 states (amounts 0..A), and each state tries k coins: O(A · k). Without memoization, the recursion re-solves the same amounts and grows exponentially, roughly O(k^A) in the worst case.

lessons.why: Dynamic programming turns exponential brute force into polynomial time. The recurse–memoize–tabulate sequence makes it a method instead of a trick.

terms.d: The same smaller question is asked many times.
The best answer is built from best answers to subproblems.
Cache recursive results so each state is computed once.
Fill a table bottom-up in an order where dependencies come first.

mistakes.wrong: DP means finding a clever formula.
mistakes.right: Start with a plain recursive solution and a clearly defined state; the rest is mechanical.

mistakes.wrong: Greedy works for coin change.
mistakes.right: With coins 1, 3 and 4, greedy pays 6 as 4+1+1 instead of 3+3. DP tries every last coin.

Recurse, memoize, tabulate, compress.
If each state depends only on the last few, keep just those.

lessons.title: 2D DP: grids & strings
lessons.objective: By the end you can define, fill and space-optimise 2D DP tables for grid paths and longest common subsequence.
concept: When a state needs two numbers, such as a grid cell `(r, c)` or a position `(i, j)` in each of two strings, the table is 2D. **Unique paths** moving only right or down: `paths[r][c] = paths[r-1][c] + paths[r][c-1]`, with every cell in the first row and first column equal to 1. Filling row by row, left to right, guarantees both dependencies are ready before they are needed. Time and space are O(rows × cols).

**Longest common subsequence**: `dp[i][j]` is the LCS length of the prefixes `a[:i]` and `b[:j]`. If `a[i-1] == b[j-1]`, extend the diagonal: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1`. Otherwise drop one character from either string: `max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`. The extra row and column of zeros, giving a table of size (m + 1) × (n + 1), represent empty prefixes and remove special cases. **Edit distance** has the same shape with three choices: insert, delete or replace.

Each row depends only on the previous row, so you can keep **two rows** (or even one, updated carefully) for O(n) space. A recipe for any 2D DP: (1) define `dp[i][j]` in words; (2) write the recurrence; (3) set the base cases; (4) choose a fill order so dependencies come first; (5) say where the answer lives, often `dp[m][n]`. Fill the table by hand for a tiny input before you code; most DP bugs are visible in a 4 × 4 table.

example.explain: `lcs` fills the table shown above, and its bottom-right cell is 3 ("ace" itself). `unique_paths` keeps a single row: before the update, `row[c]` still holds the value from the row above, and `row[c - 1]` has just been updated for the current row. Output: `3 28`.

lessons.tryit: Solve LeetCode 72 (Edit Distance): write the definition of `dp[i][j]` and the three-way recurrence as comments first, and fill the table for "horse" → "ros" by hand (the answer is 3). Then reduce your LCS to two rows and check it against the full-table version on 500 random string pairs.

questions.prompt: Why does the LCS table have size (m + 1) × (n + 1) instead of m × n?
options: Row 0 and column 0 represent empty prefixes, which are the base cases (LCS 0) and remove special cases
To store the final answer separately
To leave room for the subsequence itself
questions.explain: `dp[i][j]` describes the prefixes `a[:i]` and `b[:j]`, and i = 0 or j = 0 means an empty prefix, whose LCS is 0. Python lists are 0-indexed, which is why the code compares `a[i - 1]`.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: Row 1 becomes 1, 2, 3, 4 and row 2 becomes 1, 3, 6, 10. Equivalently, a path makes 2 down moves and 3 right moves in some order, and C(5, 2) = 10.

questions.prompt: What are the time and space complexities of the full-table LCS for strings of lengths m and n?
options: O(m · n) time, O(m · n) space
questions.explain: There are (m + 1)(n + 1) cells, each filled in O(1) and all stored. Keeping only two rows reduces the space to O(n) without changing the time. Exponential time is the cost of plain recursion without memoization.

questions.prompt: This LCS table is built with `[[0] * (n + 1)] * (m + 1)`. Why does it give wrong answers?
options: Every row is the same list object, so writing to one row changes all of them
The table is too small by one row
Lists of lists are not allowed in Python
questions.explain: Multiplying the outer list copies the reference to one inner list m + 1 times, which is the aliasing behaviour from Stage 1. Each write to `dp[i][j]` appears in every row. Build rows independently with `[[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]`.

video.title: Longest Common Subsequence Problem Visually Explained

lessons.why: Diff tools, spell-checkers and DNA alignment all use 2D DP over two strings. The same table technique solves grid path problems.

terms.d: A state needing two numbers, like a cell (r, c) or positions (i, j) in two strings.
Longest common subsequence: characters in order, not necessarily adjacent.
Fewest inserts, deletes and substitutions to turn one string into another.
Keep only the previous row when each row depends on the one above.

mistakes.wrong: A subsequence must be contiguous.
mistakes.right: That's a substring. A subsequence keeps order but can skip characters.

mistakes.wrong: I can fill the table in any order.
mistakes.right: Every cell must be filled after the cells it depends on: above, left and diagonal.

takeaways: Define `dp[i][j]` in words before writing the recurrence.
On a match, extend the diagonal; otherwise take the best of dropping a character.
Two rows are enough for most 2D DPs.

lessons.title: Greedy algorithms with a proof sketch
lessons.objective: By the end you can propose a greedy rule, try to break it with a small counterexample, and justify a correct one with an exchange argument.
concept: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step and never revisits it. When greedy is correct, it is short and fast, usually an O(n log n) sort followed by an O(n) scan. The danger is that greedy ideas often look right and are wrong. Coin change with coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6: taking the largest coin first gives 4 + 1 + 1, three coins, but 3 + 3 uses two. That is why the DP lesson solved coin change with a table.

The standard proof is an **exchange argument**: take any optimal solution, and show that you can swap its first choice for the greedy choice without making it worse; repeating the argument shows greedy is optimal. **Interval scheduling** (most non-overlapping meetings): sort by end time and take each meeting that starts after the last chosen one ends. Exchange: the greedy first meeting ends no later than the optimal's first meeting, so swapping it in leaves at least as much room for the rest.

Before coding a greedy rule, **try to break it** with a tiny input. For interval scheduling, "earliest start first" fails when one long meeting covers several short ones, and "shortest first" fails too. Greedy wins include jump game (track the farthest reachable index), gas station, merging intervals, Huffman coding, Dijkstra (always expand the closest vertex) and Kruskal. If small counterexamples break every greedy rule you can think of, switch to DP.

left.title: Greedy
points: One choice per step, never revisited
Usually O(n) or O(n log n)
Needs a proof such as an exchange argument

right.title: Dynamic programming
points: Considers every choice per state, reusing sub-answers
Correct whenever the recurrence is correct

example.explain: Sorted by end time, the greedy picks (1, 4), then (5, 7), then (8, 9): 3 meetings. In `can_jump`, the farthest reachable index gets stuck at 3, because index 3 has a jump of 0, so index 4 can never be reached. Output: `3 False`.

lessons.tryit: Solve LeetCode 435 (Non-overlapping Intervals) with the end-time greedy, and write the exchange argument as a three-sentence comment. Then write a brute force that tries every subset of up to 10 random intervals and confirm the greedy matches it on 500 cases. Finally, make the greedy sort by start time instead and find a failing input automatically.

questions.prompt: What does an exchange argument show?
options: That any optimal solution can be changed to use the greedy choice without getting worse, so greedy is optimal
That greedy is always faster than DP
That swapping two adjacent elements sorts a list
That every problem has a greedy solution
questions.explain: The argument transforms an arbitrary optimal solution, step by step, into the greedy solution without losing quality. It is a correctness proof, not a speed claim, and many problems (such as 0/1 knapsack) have no correct greedy rule.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
def greedy_coins(coins, amount):
    used = 0
    for c in sorted(coins, reverse=True):
        used += amount // c
        amount %= c
    return used

print(greedy_coins([1, 5, 10, 25], 63), greedy_coins([1, 3, 4], 6))
questions.explain: For 63 with US coins: two 25s, one 10, no 5, three 1s, 6 coins, which is optimal for that coin system. For [1, 3, 4] and 6: one 4 and two 1s, 3 coins, while the optimum is 3 + 3 = 2 coins. Greedy is correct for some coin systems and wrong for others.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of `max_meetings` on n meetings?
questions.explain: Sorting by end time costs O(n log n) and the scan is O(n), so the sort dominates. Trying every subset of meetings would be O(2^n).

questions.prompt: Which input shows that "pick the shortest meeting first" is NOT optimal for maximising non-overlapping meetings?
questions.explain: Shortest-first picks (4, 6), which overlaps both others, giving 1 meeting, while (0, 5) and (5, 10) fit together, giving 2. In the other inputs shortest-first happens to find the optimum (3, 1 and 2 meetings respectively), so they are not counterexamples.

lessons.why: Greedy algorithms are short and fast, but plausible greedy rules are often wrong. Testing and proving them is what separates a lucky answer from a correct one.

terms.d: Make the locally best choice and never revisit it.
A small input where the greedy rule gives a wrong answer.
Show any optimal solution can swap in the greedy choice without getting worse.
Pick the most non-overlapping intervals: sort by end time.

mistakes.wrong: If greedy works on my examples, it's correct.
mistakes.right: Try to break it with tiny inputs, then justify it with an exchange argument.

mistakes.wrong: For interval scheduling, take the shortest or earliest-starting meeting first.
mistakes.right: Both fail on small counterexamples. Earliest end time is the rule that's provably optimal.

Hunt for counterexamples before coding.
The exchange argument is the standard proof.

lessons.title: Backtracking: subsets & permutations
lessons.objective: By the end you can write the choose–explore–unchoose template to generate subsets, combinations and permutations, prune dead branches, and state the output-size complexity.
concept: Backtracking is DFS over a tree of choices. At each node, if the partial solution is complete, record it; otherwise, for each available choice: **choose** it (`path.append(x)`), **explore** (recurse), then **unchoose** it (`path.pop()`). Undoing the choice is what lets one `path` list be reused for the whole search instead of copying it at every step. The template fits subsets, combinations, permutations, N-Queens, Sudoku and word search.

**Subsets**: every element is either in or out, so there are 2^n subsets and generating them all costs O(n · 2^n), including the cost of copying each one. **Permutations**: any unused element can fill the next position, giving n! results and O(n · n!) time. For **combinations** and **combination sum**, pass a `start` index so you never go back to earlier elements; that prevents producing the same set in a different order, such as [1, 2] and [2, 1].

**Pruning** stops exploring a branch the moment it cannot lead to a valid answer: the running sum already exceeds the target (with candidates sorted), a queen is attacked, or the current prefix is not in a trie of words. It rarely changes the worst-case Big-O but often turns minutes into milliseconds. And always record a **copy**, `path[:]`. Appending `path` itself stores a reference to the one list that the pops will eventually empty.

visual.title: Subsets of [1, 2, 3] in the order the template records them

steps.label: Record []
steps.detail: then choose 1

steps.label: Record [1], [1, 2], [1, 2, 3]
steps.detail: keep choosing the next element

steps.label: Unchoose 3, then 2
steps.detail: choose 3 → record [1, 3]

steps.label: Back to []
steps.detail: choose 2 → record [2], [2, 3]; then choose 3 → record [3]

example.code:
def subsets(nums):
    out, path = [], []
    def bt(start):
        out.append(path[:])
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            path.append(nums[i])
            bt(i + 1)
            path.pop()
    bt(0)
    return out

def permutations(nums):
    out, path, used = [], [], [False] * len(nums)
    def bt():
        if len(path) == len(nums):
            out.append(path[:])
            return
        for i, x in enumerate(nums):
            if not used[i]:
                used[i] = True
                path.append(x)
                bt()
                path.pop()
                used[i] = False
    bt()
    return out

print(subsets([1, 2, 3]))
print(len(permutations([1, 2, 3, 4])))
example.explain: In `subsets` every node of the choice tree is a valid answer, so it records on entry; `start` ensures elements are only taken in increasing index order. `permutations` records only full-length paths and uses `used` to skip elements already placed. Output: the 8 subsets, then `24` (4!).

questions.explain: Each element is independently in or out: 2 × 2 × … × 2 = 2^n, counting the empty set and the full set. n! counts permutations, and n(n − 1)/2 counts pairs.

questions.prompt: You must find which of 10,000 dictionary words appear in a 12 × 12 letter grid (Word Search II). Which combination fits best?
options: Backtracking DFS from each cell, guided by a trie of the words so dead prefixes are pruned immediately
A separate backtracking search for each of the 10,000 words
Sort the grid letters and binary search

lessons.why: Puzzles, scheduling, configuration and search problems often require trying combinations. Backtracking explores them systematically and prunes the hopeless ones early.

terms.d: Add a choice, recurse, then undo it before trying the next.
2^n possibilities: each element in or out.
n! orderings: any unused element can go next.
Stop exploring a branch as soon as it can't lead to a valid answer.

mistakes.wrong: I can append `path` itself to the results.
mistakes.right: It keeps changing as you backtrack. Append a copy: `path[:]`.

mistakes.wrong: Pruning changes the worst-case complexity.
mistakes.right: It often helps a lot in practice, but the output-size bound (like n · 2^n) still applies.

takeaways: Backtracking is DFS over a tree of choices.
Undo every choice after exploring it.
State complexity by output size: n · 2^n subsets, n · n! permutations.

lessons.title: A repeatable problem-solving process
lessons.objective: By the end you can run a six-step process (understand, examples, brute force, optimise, code, test) on an unseen medium problem within about 30 minutes.
concept: Strong problem solvers don't wait for inspiration; they run a process. **1. Understand**: restate the problem in your own words and ask about input sizes, value ranges, duplicates, negatives, empty input, and the exact return format. **2. Examples**: work two or three by hand, including an edge case; this is where most misunderstandings surface. **3. Brute force**: state the obvious solution and its complexity out loud, even if it is too slow. It gives you a baseline and something to test against later.

**4. Optimise**: use the constraints to set a target, for example n ≤ 10^5 means O(n log n) or better. Then ask the pattern questions. What work is repeated? (hash map, prefix sums, DP) Is the input sorted, or can it be? (two pointers, binary search) Is the answer a contiguous range? (sliding window) Is it a graph in disguise? (BFS, DFS, union-find) Do I repeatedly need the best item? (heap) **5. Code**: talk as you write, use clear names, and pull pieces into helper functions.

**6. Test**: trace your code by hand on the small example, then on edge cases: empty input, one element, all equal values, the largest size. When practising, compare against your brute force on random inputs. Time-box your practice: if you are stuck after 20–25 minutes, read a solution, then re-solve it from scratch two or three days later, since spaced re-solving is how patterns stick. Log every problem in a pattern journal with the pattern, the key insight and your mistake.

steps.detail: Restate the problem; ask about sizes, ranges and edge cases

steps.label: Examples · 3 min
steps.detail: Work 2–3 by hand, including an edge case

steps.label: Brute force · 3 min
steps.detail: State it and its Big-O out loud

example.code:
import random

# Problem: ans[i] = product of every element except nums[i], without division, in O(n).
# Brute force: for each i, multiply the other n - 1 numbers: O(n^2).
# Insight: ans[i] = (product of everything left of i) * (product of everything right of i).

def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    ans = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        ans[i] = left
        left *= nums[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        ans[i] *= right
        right *= nums[i]
    return ans

def brute(nums):
    out = []
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        p = 1
        for j, x in enumerate(nums):
            if j != i:
                p *= x
        out.append(p)
    return out

for _ in range(1000):
    nums = [random.randint(-3, 3) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 6))]
    assert product_except_self(nums) == brute(nums)
print(product_except_self([1, 2, 3, 4]))
example.explain: The comments record steps 1–4: problem, brute force with its cost, and the insight that removes repeated work. The random test against the brute force (step 6) covers zeros and negatives, which hand-picked examples often miss. Output: `[24, 12, 8, 6]`.

lessons.tryit: Pick an unseen medium from the NeetCode roadmap, set a 30-minute timer, and run the six steps, writing each step's notes as comments before you write any code. Afterwards, add a journal entry: problem, pattern, time taken, solved unaided (yes/no), key insight, and the mistake you made. Repeat with a second problem from a different category.

questions.prompt: What should you do first when you get an unseen problem?
options: Restate it and clarify input sizes, edge cases and the expected output
Start coding the optimal solution straight away
Look for a similar problem online
Write the test cases for the final code
questions.explain: Understanding comes first, because a fast solution to a misread problem is worth nothing, and the constraints you clarify tell you the target complexity. Tests come last, once there is code to test.

questions.prompt: "Given an unsorted list of integers, return the length of the longest run of consecutive values (like 4, 5, 6, 7) in O(n)." Which data structure fits?
options: A hash set: start counting only from values x where x − 1 is not in the set
questions.explain: With a set, each run is counted once from its smallest value, and every membership check is O(1), giving O(n) overall. Sorting also works but costs O(n log n), which misses the stated target. A heap or stack does not help with "is x + 1 present?" questions.

questions.prompt: Using `product_except_self` from the example, what does this print?
questions.code:
def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    ans = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        ans[i] = left
        left *= nums[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        ans[i] *= right
        right *= nums[i]
    return ans

print(product_except_self([2, 0, 4]))
questions.explain: After the left pass, ans = [1, 2, 0]. The right pass multiplies by the products to the right: ans[2] = 0 × 1, ans[1] = 2 × 4 = 8, and ans[0] = 1 × (4 × 0) = 0. Only the position holding the zero gets a non-zero product.

questions.prompt: "Given meeting intervals, return the minimum number of rooms needed." Which approach fits?
options: Sort by start time and keep a min-heap of end times for rooms in use
questions.explain: Process meetings by start time. If the earliest-ending room (the heap's root) is free by then, reuse it with `heapreplace`; otherwise push a new end time. The heap's final size is the answer, in O(n log n). Union-find would count groups of overlapping meetings, not the peak number of simultaneous ones.

exam.prompt: "Count the ways to decode a digit string where 1 = A … 26 = Z." Which technique fits?
exam.explain: ways(i) = ways(i−1) (if digit i is valid on its own) + ways(i−2) (if the last two digits form 10–26). Overlapping subproblems with a recurrence call for DP. A greedy choice of one or two digits cannot count all decodings.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: One longest common subsequence is "bcba" (another is "bdab"), of length 4. The table only stores lengths; recovering the actual subsequence means walking back from dp[-1][-1].

exam.prompt: Which of these problems does a simple greedy rule solve optimally?
options: Jump game: can you reach the last index?
Coin change with arbitrary coin values
exam.explain: Tracking the farthest reachable index is provably correct for jump game. 0/1 knapsack, arbitrary coin change and LCS all have small counterexamples to every greedy rule and need DP.

exam.prompt: How many times is `fib` called?
exam.explain: Each n from 2 to 10 is computed once, and each computation makes 2 calls; together with the top-level call that is 1 + 9 × 2 = 19. Without the memo it would be 177 calls: memoization turns exponential growth into linear.

exam.prompt: How many permutations does a list of 10 distinct items have?
exam.explain: 10! = 3,628,800. 1,024 = 2^10 is the number of subsets. Generating every permutation of 10 items is feasible, but by about n = 12 (479 million) it is not.

exam.prompt: A 2D DP fills `dp[i][j]` from `dp[i-1][j]` and `dp[i][j-1]`, row by row. Why does keeping a single 1D row (as in `unique_paths`) work?
options: Before `row[j]` is overwritten it still holds `dp[i-1][j]`, and `row[j-1]` has already been updated to `dp[i][j-1]`
Because Python copies the row automatically
It doesn't work; the answer is always wrong
exam.explain: The fill order makes one array hold the previous row to the right of j and the current row to the left of j, which is exactly the two values the recurrence needs. This O(n)-space trick depends on the dependencies; a recurrence that also reads `dp[i-1][j-1]` needs a saved variable.

exam.prompt: Your O(n²) solution passes the examples, and the constraints say n ≤ 10^5. What should you do next?
options: Submit it, since it passes the examples
Estimate the work: 10^10 operations is far too slow in Python, so look for repeated work to remove with a hash map, sorting or prefix sums
exam.explain: Step 4 of the process: use the constraints to set a target (O(n log n) or better here), then find the repeated work. Passing small examples says nothing about speed. Recursion changes the code's form, not its complexity.

exam.explain: This is minimum path sum, computed in place. The cheapest route is 1 → 3 → 1 → 1 → 1 = 7 (right, right, down, down). Each cell adds the cheaper of the cells above and to its left, which are already final because of the row-by-row fill order.
